relevance_reason: Inter-SC trade mechanics in EDAM/WEIM touch settlement and bilateral procurement processes that hydro and other resource owners use to reconcile double-settlement exposures and manage revenue; the document trains SCs (scheduling coordinators, a role hydro operators typically hold) on the operational procedures for trades across the expanding regional markets.
evidence: training date — "July 7, 2026" | physical trade submission window in day-ahead market — "Submit beginning seven days prior to trade date and up to 11:00 hours the day before trade date" [UNVERIFIED] | day-ahead settlement by charge code — "Settled hourly based on corresponding physical resource pnode/apnode DA LMPs (CC 6301)" [UNVERIFIED] | real-time settlement by charge code — "Settled hourly based on the average of 4 FMM intervals on corresponding pnode/apnode LMPs" [UNVERIFIED] | market simulation structured scenario dates — "7/20/26 – 8/1/26" | connectivity testing dates — "7/6/26 – 7/19/26"
ai_summary: CAISO held a training session on July 7, 2026, introducing Scheduling Coordinators (SCs) participating in the Western Energy Imbalance Market (WEIM) and Extended Day-Ahead Market (EDAM) to inter-SC trade functionality for energy. Inter-SC trades are optional settlement services that allow two SCs to reconcile bilateral-procurement arrangements and "flip the money" to reverse double-settlement exposures, without affecting dispatch or scheduling of resources. The training covers three types of energy trades: Physical trades (PHY) backed by a generating unit, allowing submission seven days prior through 11:00 hours the day before; Aggregated Pricing Node trades (APN) at trading hubs or default load-aggregation points; and Converted Physical trades (CPT), where a PHY that exceeds the day-ahead schedule of its resource becomes a hub-based trade. Day-ahead trades are settled hourly at the resource pnode/apnode locational margin prices (Charge Code 6301); real-time trades are settled at the average of four fifteen-minute-market interval LMPs (Charge Code 6371). SCs must submit matching trades in the SIBR (Scheduling Infrastructure & Business Rules) application and continue to submit energy bids in the day-ahead and real-time markets per standard rules. A market simulation with structured scenarios is scheduled for July 20–August 1, 2026, with connectivity testing July 6–19, 2026.
hydro_read_through: The document does not mention hydropower, pumped storage, or run-of-river resources directly. However, inter-SC trades are a core settlement mechanism for dispatchable resources—including large conventional hydro and pumped-storage plants—that sell into bilateral contracts while also participating in WEIM/EDAM market-clearing. Hydro operators typically hold SC certification and use trades to manage the divergence between their contracted supply price and the nodal LMP at their resource location, a critical lever for revenue alignment across multi-zone markets. The expansion of this functionality from California ISO to WEIM and EDAM participants directly affects how hydro SCs in new member zones (PacifiCorp, Idaho Power, Puget Sound Energy, etc.) will reconcile bilateral sales with market settlement; getting the operational procedures right in simulation before the August activation date is essential to avoid settlement disputes and cash-flow mismatches on existing contracts.

ai_summary: CAISO presented a proposal to recalibrate gas resource management tools for the EDAM, addressing cost estimation and fuel procurement challenges faced by gas resources outside the ISO balancing authority area. The initiative modifies the reference-level change request process to allow more frequent use and adjusts cost thresholds for market participants whose gas hubs are more volatile than ISO calculated estimates. CAISO proposes providing additional flexibility during periods of significant forecast uncertainty (D+2→D+1 or D+1→real-time) to reflect costs of unexpected unit commitments, and creating after-the-fact cost recovery eligibility when physical supply disruptions occur after the adjustment deadline. The proposal also seeks expanded authority to use gas constraints as a reliability tool across the full ISO market footprint (currently limited to the southern part), and enhancement of the D+2 advisory market to better inform fuel procurement decisions. A 2018-approved commitment cost and default energy bid policy that was never implemented is being revisited for potential activation.
hydro_read_through: The document does not mention hydro or PSH directly. However, the changes to default energy bid and reference-level adjustment processes are the same mechanisms used to govern offer behavior and cost recovery for all use-limited resources in the ISO and EDAM. Hydro and PSH operators use these same reference-level and default energy bid tools to reflect operational costs and scarcity conditions; any liberalization of cost thresholds, frequency of adjustment requests, or after-the-fact recovery eligibility would apply to them as well. Additionally, the expansion of these tools to full EDAM participation and the relaxation of cost-recovery eligibility rules during supply disruptions could improve revenue flexibility for hydro and PSH in stressed conditions, though the proposal's primary focus on gas procurement volatility means the specific mechanics may not be optimized for hydro seasonal or hydrologic variability.

relevance_reason: CAISO's price-formation enhancements directly address scarcity pricing and market power mitigation—the core mechanisms affecting energy price formation and opportunity-cost offer development for hydro and other dispatchable resources.

ai_summary: CAISO staff briefing on the Spotlight Initiative—Price Formation Enhancements, presented to the WEM Governing Body on October 28, 2025. The briefing explains two foundational mechanisms: (1) BAA-level Market Power Mitigation (MPM), which detects and mitigates uncompetitive pricing when a balancing authority area becomes import-constrained and depends on a small number of suppliers; and (2) Scarcity Pricing, which allows prices to reflect the reliability value of reserves when available capacity is tight. The straw proposal discussed includes three BAA-level MPM changes: shift to a grouping approach testing connected BAAs together, include CAISO BAA in the test, and mitigate only pivotal suppliers to avoid unnecessary mitigation of fringe participants. For scarcity pricing, proposed changes include preserving scarcity signals to reflect opportunity cost of capacity from contingency reserves in the 5-minute market, triggering scarcity pricing for load-shedding events, and developing a comprehensive scarcity pricing design through stakeholder working groups. The briefing notes that CAISO will bring formal policy proposals to the WEM Governing Body and ISO Board of Governors for consideration in 2026.
hydro_read_through: The document does not mention hydropower or pumped storage. However, the price-formation mechanisms described directly shape how hydro's energy sales are valued in scarcity conditions and how its bids are treated under market power rules. Scarcity pricing's focus on opportunity cost of capacity and use of contingency reserves is particularly material for run-of-river and storage-constrained hydro, which face chronically imperfect pricing of their flexibility value; changes to how CAISO reflects reserve scarcity could significantly alter the energy prices hydro receives during tight conditions. BAA-level MPM changes that shift from individual-supplier tests to grouping approaches and pivot-supplier logic may reduce unnecessary mitigation of hydro bids in constrained zones, but the document does not specify how the revised framework treats use-limited resources or whether it alters the opportunity-cost reference-price methodology that has historically undervalued hydro's strategic value.

title: Briefing on Spotlight Initiative - Price Formation Enhancements - Vitol Presentation - Oct 2025
relevance_reason: Vitol's presentation directly addresses scarcity pricing and operating reserve demand curves (ORDC) as core mechanisms of energy price formation in CAISO, which govern how hydro's energy and reserve revenues are determined during shortage conditions—a foundational revenue stream for dispatchable resources.
evidence: Presentation date October 28, 2025 — "October 28, 2025 - Western Energy Markets Governing Body" | LOLP×VOLL as the design basis for ORDC — "An efficient ORDC should reflect the marginal reliability value of reserves at each shortage level, which is the VOLL * the probability of losing load LOLP*VOLL" | One-hour-ahead LOLP measurement for scarcity detection — "Measurement of the short-run probability (e.g., over the next hour) that unanticipated increases in load or decreases in available generation would reduce operating reserves below the minimum reserve level"
ai_summary: Vitol presented to CAISO's Price Formation Enhancements initiative on October 28, 2025, advocating for implementation of an enhanced operating reserve demand curve (ORDC) in both real-time and day-ahead markets. The proposal calls for scarcity pricing to reflect the reliability value of reserves using a Loss of Load Probability multiplied by Value of Lost Load (LOLP×VOLL) framework before reserve shortages occur, rather than only during load-shed events. Key design elements outlined include scarcity detection methodology (one-hour-ahead LOLP measurement), VOLL valuation based on customer data segmented by load class and outage duration, minimum contingency reserve thresholds, and reserve types to be included in the requirement. Vitol supports CAISO's initial proposal to ensure energy prices reflect shortage costs during involuntary load-shed events but argues that an enhanced ORDC would improve price signals ahead of shortages, enabling supply and demand response before constraints tighten.
hydro_read_through: The document does not name hydro or PSH, but it directly affects how dispatchable resources including conventional hydro are compensated for energy and reserve provision during tight system conditions. Enhanced scarcity pricing through LOLP×VOLL would raise energy prices more gradually and predictably as reserves tighten, creating higher and earlier price signals that reward hydro's ability to ramp quickly and sustain output. This contrasts with CAISO's current design where prices spike sharply only during declared emergencies; a continuous ORDC would increase hydro's revenue in the 10–100 hour window before physical shortages occur—precisely where hydro's marginal value is highest. The outcome depends on CAISO's adoption of this proposal and the VOLL magnitude it chooses; understating VOLL would limit the benefit.

ai_summary: CAISO's Demand and Distributed Energy Market Integration (DDEMI) initiative proposes to allow behind-the-meter exports from authorized end-use customers within a demand response aggregation to count toward measured load curtailment, provided the aggregation does not net export. Currently, individual customers net exporting (e.g., solar + battery) have their load "zeroed out" in performance calculations; the proposal would instead apply a floor at the aggregation level, capping credited demand response energy at the baseline value. The initiative also commits to convene a working group to explore real-time bidding constructs for flexible load and pumped-storage resources. The framework for net-export treatment at the aggregation level also establishes a template that could influence how future distributed-storage or hybrid rules treat exports—setting precedent for how energy exports from any co-located generation or storage facility are modeled and compensated.

ai_summary: CAISO proposes a tariff amendment to establish a cost-recovery mechanism for Regional Organization for Western Energy (ROWE) start-up debt financing. The ROWE is a new independent entity that will assume governance responsibilities over regional energy markets operated by CAISO, with the goal of promoting broader participation in WEIM and EDAM and reducing electricity costs. The ISO would guarantee a commercial loan or line of credit not to exceed $8.5 million, with repayment scheduled to begin and end during 2028. The cost-recovery mechanism establishes two new settlement charges—a market services charge and a real-time dispatch charge—modeled on existing Grid Management Charge components, allocating 68% to market services and 32% to real-time dispatch. ai_summary: The Market Surveillance Committee of CAISO issued a final opinion in December 2025 on the Gas Resource Management (GRM) proposal, examining how CAISO's mitigation of commitment-cost and energy-offer caps affects gas-fired resource participation in EDAM (Extended Day-Ahead Market), which launches in 2026. The opinion identifies four core challenges: enabling EDAM participants to reflect current gas costs in offer prices given morning-market gas purchasing deadlines, providing after-the-fact cost recovery when afternoon gas markets force higher purchases, improving day-ahead schedule forecasts (D+2) to inform morning gas procurements, and preventing locational market power abuse. ai_summary: CAISO's Board of Governors voted in October 2025 to update the ISO's default resource adequacy rules (last revised in 2006) to modernize qualifying-capacity criteria and planning-reserve-margin methodology. The proposal replaces one-size-fits-all accreditation with differentiated approaches: dispatchable hydro and run-of-river hydro will now be accredited using Average Effective Load Carrying Capability (ELCC) based on forced outage rates and generation during critical periods respectively; pumped-storage hydroelectric resources will use Unforced Capacity (UCAP) calculated from three years of historic outage data (Winter: November–April; Summer: May–October). The ISO will conduct an annual transparent process to establish values, with stakeholders (including local regulatory authorities such as CPUC, Northern California Power Agency, and Six Cities) able to adopt these defaults or set their own methodologies. The Board authorized Management to file tariff amendments with FERC. Concurrent Track 2 and Track 3 efforts will address resource adequacy availability incentives and other related provisions.
hydro_read_through: Conventional hydro owners face a material shift in capacity accreditation. The shift from historic net-dependable-capacity (NERC GADS) to average ELCC for dispatchable hydro and to ELCC based on critical-period generation for run-of-river hydro changes how much capacity a plant can offer into the market; the values will now reflect dynamic system conditions and the resource's actual contribution to meeting peak needs during scarcity events, rather than nameplate or historical-average metrics. Pumped-storage operators benefit from direct UCAP accreditation (a more straightforward outage-rate adjustment) rather than being bundled with thermal or nuclear. Annual recalculation introduces some uncertainty for multi-year revenue planning, but the transparent modeling process and CPUC coordination create opportunity to influence methodology design. The new framework is designed to align with CPUC's pending UCAP framework for 2028 implementation.

ai_summary: GridLab consultant Ed Smeloff submits comments supporting CAISO's Draft 2025-2026 Transmission Plan and proposes a Granular Scenario Planning approach for future cycles to address concentrated load growth in specific grid locations. ai_summary: CAISO presented a spotlight briefing on the Extended Day-Ahead Market (EDAM) congestion revenue allocation Phase 2 initiative to the WEM Governing Body in June 2026. Phase 2, launched December 2025, evaluates enhancements and long-term design to address potential self-scheduling incentives and asymmetry between CAISO and EDAM allocations. Three design concepts are under evaluation: (1) enhanced allocation based on cleared schedules, expanding eligibility beyond balanced self-schedules to economically bid and cleared schedules with reciprocal treatment for ISO balancing area; (2) historical baseline rights framework establishing historical transmission rights eligible for expanded congestion hedges; and (3) ongoing simultaneous feasibility framework using annual and monthly feasibility tests to assign financial entitlements to congestion revenues. The Phase 2 redesign—shifting from balanced self-schedule eligibility to economically bid schedules, and potentially using simultaneous feasibility or historical baseline frameworks—would change which hydro resources qualify for hedging and how much value they recover per MW of transmission right. Hydro operators participating in EDAM as either balancing-area resources or external participants depend on clarity around congestion-hedge rules to model inter-temporal dispatch value and transmission-dependent export strategies.

ai_summary: Joint LSEs (CalCCA, Six Cities, NCPA, PG&E, SCE) filed comments opposing adoption of expansive scarcity-pricing revisions to CAISO's Day-Ahead Market Enhancements (DAME) and Extended Day-Ahead Market (EDAM) design, specifically rejecting Vitol's and WPTF's proposals to enhance scarcity pricing using Value of Lost Load (VOLL) methodology. The LSEs argue that no need has been demonstrated for substantial modifications to scarcity-pricing measures already included in the EDAM/DAME design, citing 13 GW of storage integrated since 2020 and an interconnection queue with proposed projects several times the forecast demand volume. The LSEs oppose BAA-specific scarcity-pricing approaches and assert that any scarcity-pricing mechanism must apply uniformly across all BAAs participating in WEIM and EDAM to avoid disproportionate sub-area impacts and ensure just and reasonable rates; they call for deferring any broad scarcity-pricing modifications until initial EDAM/DAME operations can be evaluated. The comment letter was submitted October 28, 2025, to the Western Energy Markets Governing Body.
hydro_read_through: The document does not mention hydropower or storage explicitly. However, scarcity-pricing design at CAISO/WEIM/EDAM scale is foundational to hydro revenue in Western markets: the mechanism determines what price adders hydro receives during scarcity events and whether those prices apply uniformly across the multi-BAA footprint or are fragmented by balancing-authority boundary. LSEs are arguing against a VOLL-based approach and for uniform BAA-spanning pricing, which would constrain the scarcity-price ceiling hydro can receive but would prevent BAA-edge arbitrage and unfair sub-area congestion rents. If VOLL were adopted at the high levels cited from the MISO example, hydro with storage capability would benefit from higher scarcity events; if scarcity pricing remains moderate and uniform, hydro's revenue upside is lower but its market risk is more predictable and its investment case remains aligned with regional adequacy goals rather than peak-event windfall.

The treatment of opportunity outages is especially material for hydropower, which is routinely curtailed or asked to hold water for grid reliability; if such curtailments are treated as plant unavailability rather than system-requested events, seasonal and annual accreditation will be suppressed.

relevance_reason: WEIM benefits and market-update reporting establishes the value of interregional imbalance-market participation and price-formation mechanics central to Western hydropower's strategic positioning and export revenue.
evidence: $411.98 million in Q3 2025 economic benefits — "Economic benefits total $411.98 million in Q3 2025" | $7.82 billion cumulative benefits through Q3 2025 — "$7.82 billion cumulative benefits through Q3 2025" | 23 balancing areas in WEIM footprint — "Wide footprint consisting of 23 balancing areas" | Q3 2025 moderate prices remained below bilateral prices — "Real-time Western Energy Imbalance Market moderate prices remained below bilateral prices for Q3" | Congestion on transmission constraints in TID, BANC and LAWDP areas — "Higher prices in TID, BANC and LAWDP areas were driven by congestion on transmission constraints"
ai_summary: The Western Energy Imbalance Market (WEIM) delivered $411.98 million in economic benefits during Q3 2025, bringing cumulative benefits to $7.82 billion through Q3 2025. The market's 23-member footprint continues to generate large volumes of economic transfers via real-time price convergence, with moderate prices in WEIM remaining below bilateral prices in Q3. Prices trended upward following higher summer loads, with congestion on transmission constraints (notably in TID, BANC, and LAWDP areas) driving locational price variation. This market-performance update was presented to the WEM Governing Body in December 2025.
hydro_read_through: The document does not mention hydropower or pumped storage directly. However, the WEIM is a foundational strategic option for Western hydro owners: it enables real-time energy balancing across a 23-balancing-area footprint, unlocking arbitrage revenue through price convergence and allowing Northwest and other hydro-rich regions to export flexibility into higher-value areas. Congestion patterns (TID, BANC, LAWDP) signal where transmission-constrained areas value flexible ramping resources like hydro; demonstrating sustained high transfer volumes and economic benefits validates WEIM participation as an ongoing revenue stream that justifies hydro plants' operational commitments to the market.

title: Presentation - Resource Adequacy Modeling and Program Design - Track 2 - Jul 22, 2026
relevance_reason: CAISO's revised RAAIM (Resource Availability and Accuracy Incentive Mechanism) directly reshapes penalty exposure and revenue-recovery allocation for hydropower and storage resources during stress events, moving from a monthly netted assessment to per-event tiered triggers that substantially increase payoff volatility and compliance burden for use-limited resources.
initiatives: Resource adequacy modeling and program design  [Active]
stakeholders: Christina Guimera (CAISO); Matt Fulton (CAISO); Partha Malvadkar (CAISO); WPTF (Western Power Trading Forum)
ai_summary: CAISO proposes overhauling its RAAIM availability-penalty mechanism, replacing a $4.40/kW-month fixed charge assessed over monthly AAH windows with event-based tiered pricing: Tier 1 (Elevated Reliability Risk) at day-ahead LMP, and Tier 2 (Critical Capacity Insufficiency, keyed to EDAM RSE failures) at $2,000/MWh. Hydro, storage, VERs, thermal, and DR would receive technology-specific treatment: hydro and thermal face shown-RA-based availability assessment against bids and outage status; storage's obligation is tied to SDM-modeled feasibility limits and SOC nonlinearity (not automatic outage exposure); VERs are exempted from low-wind/solar/ambient variability but remain exposed for forced equipment outages. Co-located and hybrid resources receive configuration-specific rules. The proposal eliminates the <1 MW exemption and tightens exemptions overall. Stakeholder feedback flagged that storage and hydro need duration, state-of-charge, and hydrologic limits recognized; that Tier 2 exposure should reflect cost causation not any EDAM failure; and that penalty exposure must not exceed shown RA. No vote or comment deadline is stated in this presentation; next steps are listed as pending.

title: Presentation - Storage Design and Modeling - Jul 22, 2026
relevance_reason: CAISO is redesigning default energy bids for storage and hybrids, which directly affects the opportunity-cost offer framework for pumped storage and creates a precedent being leveraged across EDAM/WEIM; storage DEB is the primary mitigation-compliant bidding pathway for PSH and energy-limited resources.
initiatives: Storage design and modeling [Active]
stakeholders: Brenda Marquez (CAISO); Dinesh Das Gupta (CAISO); Sergio Dueñas Meléndez (CAISO)
ai_summary: CAISO is evaluating two methodologies to reform storage default energy bids (DEBs): a time-of-day approach that incorporates hydro DEB elements with hourly multipliers (1.4 pre-opportunity-cost hour, 1.0 after) and a static hydro-based approach. The time-of-day approach, currently preferred by CAISO, applies upward-only scaling of price proxies and addresses a core PSH challenge—that current static DEBs using day-ahead LMPs become 'stale' in real-time and prevent WEIM-only storage from accessing the DEB option at all. The time-of-day approach enables WEIM-only resources to use real-time DGAP and LMP scaling, and extends this framework consistently across EDAM and WEIM. A revised straw proposal is due September 2, 2026, with comments due September 30, 2026; final proposal is targeted for October 28, 2026. Pumped storage operators reliant on negotiated DEBs or using stale price proxies gain material upside if the time-of-day approach adopts the 1.4 multiplier on opportunity cost; conversely, stakeholders opposing time-of-day multipliers below 1.0 or favoring simpler hydro-based static methods will shape whether the structure is simplified or retained.

title: Revised Straw Proposal - Resource Adequacy Modeling and Program Design - Track-2 - Jul 17, 2026
relevance_reason: The proposal directly changes hydro's resource-adequacy availability incentive mechanism (RAAIM), outage definitions, must-offer obligations, and substitute-capacity procurement processes that govern how conventional hydropower and PSH operators get paid for and manage their RA capacity and forced/planned outages.
evidence: Comment deadline August 5, 2026 — "Please submit comments on this Revised Straw Proposal and the July 22, 2026 workshop by August 5, 2026 using the comment template on the ISO stakeholder website." | Event-based availability framework replaces static monthly RAAIM — "To address these concerns, the ISO proposed to replace the current static, monthly RAAIM structure with a more targeted, event-based availability framework." | Elimination of short-notice opportunity outages — "This proposal also introduces the elimination of short-notice opportunity outages." | RAAIM assessed only on shown RA, not above it — "If a resource offers at least its shown RA but less than its MOO, the resource would not incur revised RAAIM penalties for the MW above shown RA." | Forced-outage substitution ranged 0-1% in Jun-Oct 2022 — "For June to October 2022 the average substitution for forced outages ranged between zero to one percent." | Current RAAIM penalty $4.40/kW-month far below bilateral market prices — "The current RAAIM penalty ($4.40/kW-month) is far below bilateral trading prices"
initiatives: Resource adequacy modeling and program design  [Active]
ai_summary: CAISO's Resource Adequacy Modeling and Program Design (RAMPD) Track 2 Revised Straw Proposal (July 17, 2026) proposes replacing the current static, monthly RAAIM structure with an event-based availability framework that assesses availability during periods of elevated reliability risk rather than averaging across all availability assessment hours in a month. The proposal introduces three outage classifications — planned (maintenance/construction with advance notice), urgent (increased risk but still operable), and forced (little/no notice) — and eliminates short-notice opportunity outages. It proposes a "shopping cart" workflow for substitute-capacity trading among scheduling coordinators (displayed in CIRA with seller confirmation) rather than ISO-centralized matching, and revises must-offer and RAAIM settlement rules so resources are penalized only on shown RA capacity, not on capacity above their shown RA. Comments on the proposal are due August 5, 2026.
hydro_read_through: Conventional hydropower, being inherently use-limited and weather-dependent, is highly sensitive to changes in when availability is assessed and how forced outages are treated in RA revenue. The shift from monthly averaging to event-based assessment during stressed-system conditions could concentrate RAAIM penalties on the hours hydro actually needs to be on-line (typically summer peaks), rather than diluting them across the whole month; this could either increase or decrease a hydro owner's exposure depending on how the final "elevated reliability risk" periods are defined. The new urgent-outage category and elimination of short-notice opportunity outages may reduce hydro's flexibility to take unplanned maintenance on short notice without RA penalty, making forced-outage rates and substitute-capacity costs more material to revenue; conversely, the revised RAAIM rule limiting penalties to shown RA (not MOO) could reduce exposure if a plant shows less than its full nameplate. The substitute-capacity shopping-cart mechanism replaces bilateral searching with a platform tool, but the document does not specify whether hydro, as a fast-ramping resource, would face different availability-assessment hours or outage-substitution priorities than thermal or battery resources.

title: Straw Proposal - Storage Design and Modeling - Uplift, Default Energy Bids, and State-of-Charge Management - July 15, 2026
relevance_reason: CAISO straw proposal on storage default energy bids, uplift, and state-of-charge bidding paradigms directly addresses revenue mechanisms (bid cost recovery, default energy bid methodology, opportunity-cost pricing) that apply to storage resources generally, including pumped-storage hydro, and establishes market-design precedent for how dispatchable, use-limited resources participate in the ISO market.
evidence: CAISO proposes a time-of-day approach to storage default energy bids — "To address this, the ISO details two approaches: a time-of-day approach and a static approach. After comparing both approaches to the status quo, the ISO concludes that the time-of-day approach can meet the principles for enhancement while remaining implementable." | Hybrid default energy bid approach uses a 'greater-of' method — "Ultimately, the ISO proposes to move forward with a "greater-of" method, where the default bid is based on the highest cost component, with guardrails." | ISO plans comprehensive uplift redesign by end of 2026 — "the ISO plans to use the outcomes of these near-term efforts and data from recently implemented real-time bid cost recovery changes to support a more comprehensive evaluation of uplift design. The Storage Design and Modeling initiative is therefore structured to release a draft final proposal integrating default energy bids, bidding enhancements, and uplift considerations by the end of 2026." [UNVERIFIED] | Stakeholder comment deadline is August 5, 2026 — "This paper will be discussed at a stakeholder meeting scheduled for July 22, 2026. Comments on the paper and the stakeholder meeting will be due August 5, 2026." | Storage capacity in CAISO footprint reached 16,531 MW as of June 1, 2026 — "In the ISO, storage capacity has skyrocketed from about 500 MW in 2020 to 16,531 MW as of June 1, 2026." | WEIM battery capacity was 8,500 MW at end of 2025, up 69% from late 2024 — "In the multistate Western Energy Imbalance Market (WEIM), battery capacity was 8,500 MW at the end of 2025, an increase of 69% percent compared to late 2024."
initiatives: Storage design and modeling [Active]
ai_summary: CAISO proposes enhancements to storage resource participation in energy and ancillary-services markets through three pathways: (1) replacement of the current static storage default energy bid with a time-of-day approach that incorporates temporal cost differentiation while remaining administratively implementable; (2) extension of default energy bid rules to hybrid resources using a "greater-of" method based on the highest-cost component with minimum-share guardrails; and (3) a reframing of non-generator resource bidding to allow storage to submit a single terminal state-of-charge bid reflecting willingness to pay/accept for ending an optimization period with higher or lower energy stored, relative to a reference state, rather than interval-by-interval bid curves. The ISO sequences default energy bid and bidding-structure improvements as near-term work, with a comprehensive uplift (bid cost recovery) redesign to follow by end of 2026. Comments are due August 5, 2026, following stakeholder discussion on July 22, 2026.
hydro_read_through: The document does not name hydropower or pumped storage directly; however, it addresses storage resource market participation rules that apply categorically to all use-limited storage, which includes conventional hydropower and pumped-storage facilities. The three proposed changes would affect how storage operators recover costs and value state-of-charge opportunity costs: default energy bid improvements would permit more frequent cost reassessment reflecting daily price variation (directly important for run-of-river and seasonal hydro), the hybrid framework would govern hydro paired with solar or wind, and the terminal state-of-charge bidding concept would replace the current hourly bidding structure with a single value-of-energy offer that propagates backward through dispatch optimization. The sequencing of default energy bid reform ahead of uplift redesign signals that CAISO is treating marginal-cost recovery as foundational to any future changes to bid cost recovery policy—a framework within which conventional hydro has historically received mitigation treatment as a canonical use-limited resource. The reframing concept would also change how day-ahead and real-time dispatch treat state-of-charge deviation, potentially affecting the price-following incentives that hydro operators currently use to manage storage-like flexibility.

title: WPTF Presentation - UCAP Implementation and RAAIM - Jul 22, 2026
relevance_reason: MECHANISM: UCAP implementation and RAAIM redesign directly affect how CAISO accredits and pays hydro/PSH capacity in resource-adequacy showings, and how availability is measured and penalized — touching both the accreditation revenue stream (through changes to counting rules, must-offer obligations, and deliverability ceilings) and compliance obligations (RAAIM performance metrics and penalty exposure).
initiatives: Resource adequacy modeling and program design  [Active]
stakeholders: Carrie Bentley (Western Power Trading Forum (WPTF)); Kallie Wells (Western Power Trading Forum (WPTF))
ai_summary: WPTF presents CAISO's path to implement CPUC-adopted UCAP (Unforced Capacity) methodology for 2028 RA year, arguing that CAISO must define separate capacity values post-UCAP — Pmax, PmaxRA (deliverable accredited capacity), LRA-specific QC, maximum NQC, and shown RA — because one value cannot serve every CAISO function (forward counting, deliverability studies, must-offer formulas, RAAIM exposure, exports, and backstop procurement) without double-counting or losing capability. On RAAIM, WPTF argues the current design does not need redesign: forced-outage data show no correlation with load or prices, UCAP itself does not justify price increases, and a 94.5% monthly availability floor is conceptually consistent with UCAP's removal of expected outages from the forward MW value. The presentation urges CAISO to establish demonstrated failure (via resource availability trends, substitution-request analysis, and event-level causation) before changing RAAIM penalties or exposures. This touches hydro and PSH by redefining which capacity value applies to RA accreditation, must-offer, and RAAIM calculations — especially for partially deliverable resources and storage with variable seasonal contribution — and by proposing to keep RAAIM pricing unchanged while clarifying what 'shown RA' means, which will determine both the compliance exposure and the RA revenue hydro owners receive in forward showings.

title: Presentation - Price Formation Enhancements - Scarcity Pricing - Jul 14, 2026
relevance_reason: CAISO's scarcity pricing proposal directly affects energy price formation during system stress, which is a primary revenue mechanism for hydro and pumped-storage resources that supply emergency flexibility and reserves.
ai_summary: CAISO's Revised Straw Proposal on scarcity pricing (Day 2 of Phase 2 Price Formation Enhancements, July 14, 2026) modifies two mechanisms: (1) load-shed pricing extends the scarcity signal into both real-time dispatch (RTD) and 15-minute forecasting markets (FMM) when a BAA enters EEA Level 3 emergency and operators shed firm load, treating curtailed load as unserved demand to prevent market prices from collapsing; and (2) armed-reserve pricing adds an opportunity-cost adder in RTD to reflect when reserve capacity is released into energy markets, capturing the scarcity value that the 15-minute ancillary-service procurement (RTPD) process already recognizes. Both mechanisms include operational safeguards: operators can pause either mechanism, and the load-shed signal turns off after four cumulative hours of load shedding in a 24-hour window. The proposal defers comprehensive scarcity redesign to a future phase. Feedback on grouping, CAISO BAA treatment, load-shedding implementation options (verified MW vs. forecast approach), and whether the mechanisms adequately preserve scarcity signals without over-mitigation is requested before the draft final proposal.

title: Presentation - Price Formation Enhancements - BAA-Level Market Power Mitigation - Jul 13, 2026
relevance_reason: BAA-level market power mitigation (MPM) redesign directly affects how hydro's market-power-limited capacity is tested and mitigated during scarcity — grouping, load-serving obligation subtraction, and pivotal-supplier filtering all reshape the offer floor and mitigation surface for dispatchable resources with geographically-dispersed generation or storage.
initiatives: Price formation enhancements [Active]
ai_summary: CAISO's Revised Straw Proposal reforms BAA-level MPM by grouping BAAs via Marginal Export Capacity and export-transfer connectivity (instead of testing each in isolation), subtracting interval-specific load-serving obligations from withholdable capacity, and mitigating only pivotal suppliers after a grouped BAA fails the 3PS test. CAISO BAA retains default-competitive status and will not be subject to the BAA-level test as a group — a deferent to concerns that economic intertie imports are undervalued by the current framework. The proposal advances grouping and LSO changes near-term but defers comprehensive scarcity pricing and CAISO BAA mitigation to a broader future phase, with Day 2 stakeholder feedback to focus on scarcity-pricing mechanics, implementation choices, and safeguards. For hydro operators, especially those with multi-BAA footprints or export capability (e.g., Northwest PSH and reservoir operators), the grouping and LSO logic could narrow the suppliers subject to mitigation during tight intervals, raising energy prices and ancillary-service value when genuinely pivotal capacity is constrained — but the deferral of scarcity pricing means no new scarcity-pricing adders are being adopted yet. Most exposed: large dispatchable generators and PSH with withholdable capacity in grouped BAAs; comment deadline not stated in document.

ai_summary: CAISO's May 2026 EDAM performance report documents the first month of operations across the expanded day-ahead footprint (CAISO, PacifiCorp East, PacifiCorp West), including two new products: imbalance reserves (IRU/IRD) and reliability capacity (RCU/RCD). Hydro operators see direct implications: (1) imbalance reserve procurement in PACW was supplied primarily by transfers and hydro, while reliability capacity pricing trends lower than energy and varies sharply by area, reshaping the value of flexible capacity; (2) GHG allocation reached 256 MW peak and is now BAA-specific rather than system-wide, affecting export economics from non-California balancing areas; (3) ancillary-services cascading frequency changed (regulation-up cascading fell from 28.8% to 4.7%), with spin cascading rising to 85.6%, altering the stacking and pricing of traditional AS products hydro supplies. Energy prices showed regional separation (PACE lowest, PACW higher, CAISO highest), and transfer flows indicate active cross-BAA dispatch. This is preliminary first-month data; no member action deadlines are stated in the report itself.

ai_summary: CAISO's DDEMI Track 1 proposal would allow demand response aggregations to include behind-the-meter exports from utility-authorized end-use customers (e.g., rooftop solar + battery, behind-the-meter pumped storage), while capping the aggregation's net export at the resource level rather than the individual-customer level. Stakeholders have until July 16, 2026 to submit written comments; the proposal applies to both Proxy Demand Resource (PDR) and Reliability Demand Response Resource (RDRR) models across all BAAs.

stakeholders: Ryan Kurlinski (CAISO Department of Market Monitoring)
ai_summary: CAISO's Department of Market Monitoring reports Q2 2025 real-time market conditions: electricity prices in the West rose 12% versus Q2 2024, driven by south-to-north congestion and California greenhouse-gas costs; Northwest prices were higher during solar hours, California during non-solar hours—indicating hydro's value shifts with solar generation patterns. WEIM transfer congestion into or out of Pacific Northwest areas occurred over 20% of 5-minute intervals, and Mid-Columbia and Palo Verde bilateral prices converged with ISO market prices, suggesting arbitrage opportunities narrowed. Pacific Northwest coal output rose despite more outages, and transfers from the Intermountain West during non-solar hours declined Q-o-Q, signaling reduced availability or changed dispatch incentives. For hydro owners, these trends show tightening price signals in hydro-export corridors, persistent congestion reducing transmission access to California, and seasonal shifts in the regional generation stack that affect dispatch positioning and revenue timing.

meeting_title: Comments due - On-Peak Deliverability Assessment Methodology Refinements
title: Draft - On-Peak Deliverability Study Methodology - Jun 03, 2026
relevance_reason: CAISO refines its on-peak deliverability assessment methodology — the mechanism by which generators (including hydro and storage) qualify for full or partial capacity credit toward resource adequacy; changes to Pmax assumptions, scenario hours, and dispatch modeling directly affect how much RA capacity hydro and pumped storage can claim and at what cost.
ai_summary: CAISO has refined its generator on-peak deliverability study methodology, effective January 2024 and documented here as of June 2026, to address bottleneck risk as the generation fleet diversifies and solar penetration shifts peak net load. The methodology now assesses two distinct scenarios: (1) highest system need (hours 19–22 in summer, peak sale with low solar), where non-intermittent generators' Pmax is set to highest summer Qualifying Capacity in the prior three years, and intermittent generators at 20% exceedance level; and (2) secondary system need (hours 15–18, peak consumption with high solar output), where Pmax for intermittent resources is 50% exceedance level and energy storage Pmax is 50% of 4-hour discharge capacity. For hybrid and energy-storage projects, Pmax is limited by requested maximum output. Hydro and pumped-storage owners face a direct revenue impact: the Pmax values used in deliverability studies directly determine how much capacity credit they can claim in RA markets and interconnection queues; storage capacity credit in secondary scenarios is capped at half the 4-hour discharge rating, potentially disadvantaging long-duration or seasonal storage relative to short-duration batteries.

meeting_title: Comments due - On-Peak Deliverability Assessment Methodology Refinements
title: Presentation - On-peak Deliverability Assessment Methodology Refinements - Jun 11, 2026
relevance_reason: CAISO is refining its on-peak deliverability assessment methodology—a transmission planning process that determines whether new generation (including hydro and storage) can physically deliver power to load, directly affecting the deliverability accreditation and interconnection pathway for proposed hydro and PSH projects.
ai_summary: CAISO proposes three refinements to its on-peak deliverability assessment methodology: (1) modeling proposed resources identified in transmission planning as needed for local reliability in the base case dispatch (rather than only when they relieve constraints), conditional on reasonable certainty of completion before deliverability is needed; (2) including existing demand response in the base case to avoid over-allocating deliverability; and (3) reducing the dispatch value of generators in the base case from 80% to 70% of maximum study amount to reflect the increased planning reserve margin (from ~15% to 25%). The refinements affect how new hydro and PSH projects are studied during interconnection—projects that would need to compete with modeled proposed resources to secure a deliverable position in queue. Comments are due June 25, 2026. Most exposed are developers of new hydro or PSH seeking interconnection in California who will compete for deliverability allocation against projects CAISO assumes will be built to meet identified local needs.

title: Final Market Surveillance Committee Opinion - Extended Day-Ahead Market Congestion Revenue Allocation - Jun 16, 2025
relevance_reason: EDAM congestion revenue allocation rules directly affect how hydro operators recover transmission-congestion hedges and how parallel-flow costs from hydro schedules are reallocated across balancing authorities — a core revenue-protection mechanism for dispatchable and use-limited resources in the Western interregional market.
stakeholders: Benjamin F. Hobbs (Market Surveillance Committee, CAISO (paid consultant)); James Bushnell (Market Surveillance Committee, CAISO (paid consultant)); Scott M. Harvey (Market Surveillance Committee, CAISO (paid consultant))
ai_summary: The CAISO Market Surveillance Committee issued a final opinion (June 16, 2025) on EDAM's proposed congestion revenue allocation scheme for parallel flows, evaluating a Year 1 interim design that would reallocate congestion revenues from BAAs where congestion occurs to BAAs that sold firm point-to-point and NITS transmission rights when those holders self-schedule. The MSC has significant reservations about the Year 1 design because it creates perverse incentives to self-schedule instead of participating in economically efficient co-optimized dispatch, potentially distorting bidding and causing unintended cost shifts — a concern particularly acute for hydro and other dispatchable resources whose flexibility value depends on competitive economic dispatch. The opinion does not block the proposal but calls for detailed pre-EDAM-launch empirical analysis of dispatch distortion and market-price effects from self-scheduling incentives, and notes that Year 2 alternatives linked to flexibly-bid resources would worsen below-cost-offer incentives; the framework recommended for future exploration is financial flowgate rights rather than transaction-linked reallocation.

title: Final Market Surveillance Committee Opinion on Gas Resource Management - Dec 15, 2025
relevance_reason: CAISO's Gas Resource Management proposal affects how gas-fired resources' commitment costs and default energy bids are calculated — reference levels that are the canonical mitigation tool for use-limited resources including hydropower, and directly impact EDAM participation by Western resources including hydro operators in the WEIM/EDAM footprint.
stakeholders: Sylvie Spewak (CAISO); Benjamin F. Hobbs (Market Surveillance Committee, CAISO); James Bushnell (Market Surveillance Committee, CAISO); Scott M. Harvey (Market Surveillance Committee, CAISO)
ai_summary: The CAISO Market Surveillance Committee issued a final opinion (Dec. 12, 2025) supporting three of four enhancements in CAISO's Gas Resource Management proposal: improved reference-level change-request processes, expanded after-the-fact cost-recovery rules, and multi-day advisory dispatch forecasts to help gas resources anticipate EDAM schedules and procure fuel more efficiently ahead of morning gas nominations. The MSC supports these changes to address EDAM coordination challenges as EDAM expands westward. However, the MSC emphasizes a critical gap: the absence of any market-power test for commitment-cost mitigation means all gas units are indiscriminately mitigated in every dispatch interval, creating inefficient offer bounds that may favor units with actual market power while constraining flexible suppliers. The MSC calls development of a workable commitment-cost market-power test "long overdue and should be a high priority." This is material to hydro owners because reference-level design directly affects whether hydro (a canonical use-limited resource) can offer flexibility without artificial caps, and the expansion of EDAM brings Western hydro into closer coordination with gas-constrained EDAM pricing and scheduling — misaligned gas-cost accounting upstream could distort the scarcity signals and ancillary-service values hydro depends on.

title: MSC Final Opinion - Rules for Bidding Above the Soft Offer Cap - Price Formation Enhancements - May 2024
relevance_reason: CAISO proposes revisions to Order 831 soft-offer-cap rules for battery storage and hydropower, directly affecting how energy-limited resources price their opportunity costs and manage state of charge — a core revenue mechanism for hydro and especially pumped storage.
stakeholders: Benjamin F. Hobbs (Market Surveillance Committee of the California ISO); James Bushnell (Market Surveillance Committee of the California ISO); Scott M. Harvey (Market Surveillance Committee of the California ISO)
ai_summary: The CAISO Market Surveillance Committee (MSC) issued a final opinion (May 15, 2024) supporting CAISO's proposed changes to Order 831 bidding rules for summer 2024, specifically allowing battery storage and hydropower to bid above the $1000/MWh soft cap by reflecting future-hour opportunity costs rather than only same-hour alternatives. The MSC found that current rules force premature discharge and systematic underestimation of stored energy value, creating inefficiencies that risk curtailments under tight supply conditions; the root problem is that Order 831's Maximum Import Bid Price (MIBP) mechanism was designed for thermal resources and mischaracterizes the temporal opportunity cost of energy-limited resources. The changes apply to both CAISO and Western EIM resources; the MSC also flagged that deeper reforms to local market power mitigation as applied to energy-limited resources and the real-time market's 75-minute offer-update lag remain unresolved and require future work, but the summer 2024 proposal is a necessary interim step.

title: MSC Final Opinion on Extended Day-Ahead Market
relevance_reason: EDAM's day-ahead market coordination across western balancing areas directly affects hydro's revenue from inter-BAA energy and reserve arbitrage, co-optimization of dispatch across large footprints, and participation incentives for flexible resources like pumped storage; the MSC opinion on RSE, GHG accounting, and transmission design shapes whether hydro's scarcity-pricing and flexibility value is preserved or diluted in the expanded market.
stakeholders: Benjamin F. Hobbs (CAISO Market Surveillance Committee); James Bushnell (CAISO Market Surveillance Committee); Scott M. Harvey (CAISO Market Surveillance Committee)
ai_summary: The CAISO Market Surveillance Committee issues a final opinion (January 27, 2023) endorsing the Extended Day-Ahead Market (EDAM) as a beneficial expansion of RTO-style coordination into a day-ahead voluntary market across western BAAs, while flagging unresolved design ambiguities in resource-sufficiency evaluation (RSE), greenhouse-gas accounting, and inter-BAA transmission pricing that require detailed simulation before implementation. The MSC emphasizes that EDAM will pool scarcity pricing and reserve requirements across participants—meaning a shortage in one BAA will raise prices and impose reserve penalties across the entire footprint—and notes that design choices allowing bilateral contracts and demand-reduction programs to count toward RSE requirements, combined with pooled WEIM RSE treatment, could create perverse incentives for resource-insufficient BAAs to lean on the pool. For hydro and PSH operators, EDAM's inter-BAA optimization and removal of 'pancaking' transmission charges will increase dispatch flexibility and inter-regional arbitrage opportunities, but the MSC warns that unresolved details on export constraints, shortfall allocation (especially when multiple BAAs cannot meet their EDAM schedules simultaneously), and GHG export formulation could materially affect scarcity-pricing signals and the value of flexible ramping; the committee recommends flexibility in software design to allow parameter adjustments as EDAM begins operations with an initial small set of BAAs and expands.

title: Market Surveillance Committee Addendum to Final Opinion on Day-Ahead Market Enhancements
relevance_reason: CAISO's Imbalance Reserves cost-allocation mechanism affects how hydro and storage operators are charged for uncertainty-procurement costs and how those costs flow through nodal pricing and congestion settlement — touching energy revenue and price-formation outcomes.
stakeholders: Benjamin F. Hobbs (Market Surveillance Committee of CAISO); James Bushnell (Market Surveillance Committee of CAISO); Scott M. Harvey (Market Surveillance Committee of CAISO)
ai_summary: The Market Surveillance Committee clarifies its May 2023 opinion on CAISO's Day-Ahead Market Enhancements (DAME), specifically correcting its description of how Imbalance Reserves (IR) costs will be allocated across Balancing Area Authorities. IR costs are now understood to be calculated per BAA based on nodal prices and cleared quantities of uncertainty, less payments for IR supplied at locations within the BAA — with net charges/payments aggregated across the EDAM and any resulting congestion rents allocated to transfer and transmission constraints in the same manner as energy-flow congestion. This nodal cost-allocation mirrors energy settlements, making the mechanism transparent and competitively neutral. For hydro and PSH operators, this clarification is material because it determines how uncertainty-procurement costs flow through the nodal price signal they face and how their own IR supplies (especially from PSH) are valued and credited at their location — affecting both the cost side of operations and the compensation for flexibility supply.

title: Market Surveillance Committee Final Opinion - Storage Bid Cost Recovery - Nov 01, 2024
relevance_reason: CAISO proposes changes to real-time bid cost recovery (BCR) calculations for battery storage, directly affecting how storage resources recover losses and manage state-of-charge — a canonical storage-revenue mechanism that sets precedent for pumped-storage participation and cost allocation in real-time markets.
stakeholders: Benjamin F. Hobbs (Market Surveillance Committee, California Independent System Operator); James Bushnell (Market Surveillance Committee, California Independent System Operator); Scott M. Harvey (Market Surveillance Committee, California Independent System Operator)
ai_summary: CAISO's Market Surveillance Committee (MSC) evaluates CAISO's revised proposal to modify real-time bid cost recovery for storage resources, targeting elimination of 'phantom losses' — BCR payments on losses that don't reflect actual economic harm — and improving incentives for storage operators to manage state-of-charge efficiently across the day. The MSC conditionally supports implementation of CAISO's draft final proposal as a near-term check on inflated BCR but notes that empirical data on phantom-loss materiality is incomplete; the MSC recommends immediate follow-up in Phase II to achieve deeper reforms and eliminate BCR on phantom losses before expanding storage bidding flexibility. Pumped-storage owners relying on cost-recovery mechanisms for charging losses and state-of-charge management should monitor whether CAISO's approach—which changes how discharge offers and charging bids factor into BCR calculations—narrows or preserves their ability to recover legitimate operating losses, and should engage if Phase II designs begin to collapse BCR scope more broadly.

title: Market Surveillance Committee Final Opinion on Day-Ahead Market Enhancements
relevance_reason: CAISO's Day-Ahead Market Enhancements (DAME) proposal fundamentally restructures co-optimization of energy and flexibility products, creating new imbalance-reserve procurement rules and state-of-charge constraints on storage that directly affect how pumped-storage hydro earns revenue from flexibility supply and interact with residual unit commitment pricing.
stakeholders: Benjamin F. Hobbs (Market Surveillance Committee, CAISO); James Bushnell (Market Surveillance Committee, CAISO); Scott M. Harvey (Market Surveillance Committee, CAISO)
ai_summary: CAISO's Market Surveillance Committee (MSC) issued a final opinion on May 3, 2023, supporting the Day-Ahead Market Enhancements proposal, which introduces a new Imbalance Reserves (IR) co-optimized product to replace ad-hoc operator load-biasing, updates residual unit commitment into a Reliability Capacity (RC) process, and improves storage state-of-charge modeling in day-ahead and RUC runs. The proposal moves forward with stated intent to consult stakeholders during testing and implementation, but the MSC identifies substantial untested elements: nodal IR demand-curve calculation, locational uncertainty estimation, IR deliverability constraints, and storage state-of-charge equation parameters all lack operational precedent outside CAISO and may require rapid iterative adjustment. Pumped-storage operators face direct exposure through IR constraints limiting 30-minute rampable capacity supply, storage participation rules in IR procurement, and potential changes to RUC/RC pricing interaction; the design's success depends on whether operators' flexibility needs are genuinely met by IR pricing or whether hidden costs migrate to uplift.

ai_summary: CAISO's Market Surveillance Committee issues a final opinion supporting the DAME proposal (as of May 3, 2023), which introduces a co-optimized imbalance reserve (IR) product, updates the residual unit commitment (RUC) into a reliability capacity (RC) process, and improves storage state-of-charge modeling in day-ahead and hour-ahead optimization. The MSC emphasizes substantial testing before implementation and calls for a rapid-cycle monitoring and tuning process (not traditional multi-year stakeholder proceedings) to adapt IR quantity calculations, penalty values, and storage state-of-charge parameters — all of which will materially affect PSH flexibility revenue and constraints on charging energy treatment. Implementation timing and parameter lock-in deadlines are not specified in this excerpt, but the opinion signals that CAISO will move faster than historical pace, exposing PSH and long-duration hydro to mid-course design changes.

title: Market Surveillance Committee Update - May 2023
relevance_reason: CAISO's Day-Ahead Market Enhancements (DAME) proposal directly affects energy price formation, imbalance-reserve procurement (a ramping/flexibility product), storage state-of-charge modeling, and resource-adequacy interactions — all core revenue and operational mechanisms for hydro and pumped storage in CAISO's footprint and the emerging west-wide EDAM.
stakeholders: Benjamin F. Hobbs (CAISO Market Surveillance Committee); James Bushnell (CAISO Market Surveillance Committee); Scott M. Harvey (CAISO Market Surveillance Committee)
ai_summary: The CAISO Market Surveillance Committee (MSC) issued a May 4, 2023 opinion supporting the Day-Ahead Market Enhancements (DAME) initiative, which proposes new co-optimized imbalance-reserve products, updates to residual unit commitment (RUC), and improved storage state-of-charge modeling to replace ad-hoc operator load-biasing and improve market transparency. The MSC endorses the proposal as a necessary step toward a west-wide day-ahead market (EDAM) but flags substantial uncertainties: nodal imbalance-reserve calculation methods, storage state-of-charge parameter-setting, and 30-minute ramp-constraint limits on reserve supply are untested design elements with no precedent in other RTOs. The MSC recommends conservative implementation with guardrails, pre-implementation software testing, and a rapid feedback cycle with stakeholders to adapt the design; the imbalance-reserve demand curve — which caps up-reserve prices at $55/MWh and sets penalty values influencing energy prices — will be critical to monitor. Hydro and pumped-storage operators should track parameter tuning during testing and go-live, as the storage state-of-charge equations and imbalance-reserve locational requirements will reshape the value of flexibility and multi-hour discharge capability; the MSC notes this framework has no ISO precedent and will evolve based on operational experience.

ai_summary: CAISO Market Surveillance Committee presentation analyzing the potential impact of the revised Congestion Revenue Allocation (CRA) methodology on historical WEIM congestion patterns ahead of Extended Day Ahead Market (EDAM) go-live. The analysis examines three scenarios: (1) exercise of transmission rights for PACE-to-PACW transfers, estimated to generate $2.34 to $6.96 million per month in congestion rents depending on transfer-capability assumptions (300 MW to 1200 MW); (2) incentives for self-scheduling internal generation in PacifiCorp areas, estimated at $2.2 million per month in 2024 and $1.1 million in 2025; and (3) resulting counter-flow payments of approximately $1 million per month at maximum transfer levels. The ISO committed to further analysis of revised CRA methodology impacts prior to EDAM go-live, with phase-one findings published in December 2025. Congestion rents are highly concentrated in a small number of transmission constraints, with 87–95 percent accruing to the top 20 constraints. The assessment uses historical WEIM real-time congestion and shift factors as proxies, with caveats that real-time congestion may exceed day-ahead levels and not all WEIM elements directly transfer to EDAM pricing.
hydro_read_through: The document does not name hydropower or pumped-storage facilities directly, but the CRA methodology analysis is material to hydro owners because PacifiCorp's generators in both PACE and PACW areas—which include conventional and run-of-river hydro resources—will be subject to these transmission-right and self-scheduling incentives in EDAM. The estimated monthly congestion rent flows ($1.6–$2.5 million and upward) represent revenue that will accrue to or be charged against PacifiCorp-area generators under the revised allocation rule, affecting the financial case for dispatch and transmission-constrained operation of existing hydro units. The concentration of rents in a handful of constraints means hydro output dispatch will be economically sensitive to specific transmission bottlenecks under the new regime.

ai_summary: CAISO's configurable-parameters working group completed sensitivity analyses on five EDAM design parameters: envelope constraint multiplier, IR bid cap, IR/RC default availability bids, deployed imbalance reserve factor, and transmission constraint enforcement. Key findings: higher envelope multipliers reduce battery IR procurement and raise IR prices (storage-specific impact); DIR factor and constraint enforcement interact to affect congestion and local pricing; bid caps temper clearing prices. Parallel operations (extended through April 30, 2026) will test envelope multipliers (starting at 85%, assessing lower values), DIR factor (starting at 100%, assessing reductions), and transmission constraint enforcement hierarchies; IR bid cap and DAB cap remain fixed at $55 per tariff. For pumped-storage operators, the envelope multiplier and DIR factor tuning during parallel ops directly affects how much IR PSH can procure and at what price — these govern the opportunity-cost treatment of state-of-charge constraints. Results will be assessed using parallel-ops market cases; no go-live decision date is stated, but the extended parallel window and commitment to post-go-live monitoring suggests continued parameter adjustment risk through mid-2026.

relevance_reason: EDAM congestion revenue allocation design directly affects how hydro and other dispatchable resources' energy sales are priced and settled across the Western balancing-area seam; Phase 2 evaluation of self-schedule incentives and parallel-flow revenue allocation will reshape revenue capture for hydro exports and intra-EDAM transactions.
ai_summary: CAISO is executing Phase 2 of EDAM congestion revenue allocation design, following FERC's August 2025 approval of a transitional Phase 1 design that launched EDAM in May 2026. The Phase 1 design allocates internal constraint congestion to the balancing area where the constraint sits, and allocates parallel-flow congestion from balanced self-schedules to the exercising balancing area. Phase 2 stakeholder working groups (two sessions completed as of this presentation) are now evaluating design concepts to address two key issues: (1) eliminating or reducing self-schedule incentives that discourage economic bidding, and (2) creating further symmetry in parallel-flow congestion allocation for the CAISO balancing area. The Market Surveillance Committee recommends exploring a negotiated-entitlement approach and has flagged questions about how negotiated entitlements would apply to Western market structures, existing inter-balancing-area operational agreements managing loop flow, and the basis for establishing entitlements (historical flows, dollar limits, etc.). The next phase of stakeholder working groups runs late March through May 2026. Hydro operators exporting across EDAM seams or managing run-of-river dispatch with balanced schedules face direct revenue exposure: parallel-flow congestion allocation affects the net LMP received, and the Phase 2 pivot away from self-schedule incentives toward economic bidding may reshape the value of storage and flexible hydro in managing loop-flow congestion. Owners of reservoir hydro with flexible dispatch and pumped-storage facilities in the Western Interconnection are most exposed.

title: Presentation - Extended Day-Ahead Market (EDAM) Imbalance Reserve Costs Market Surveillance Committee - Feb 06, 2026
relevance_reason: EDAM imbalance reserve market design and pricing directly affects storage and dispatchable hydro revenue from flexibility products and reserve provision; the analysis identifies design choices (15-minute start constraint, 30-minute ramp limits, 0.85 attenuation factor for storage energy usage, reserve procurement levels) that materially drive up reserve costs and reshape which resources are economical to deploy.
stakeholders: Scott Harvey (California ISO Market Surveillance Committee)
ai_summary: Scott Harvey (Market Surveillance Committee member) presents analysis of EDAM imbalance reserve pricing in simulations, finding average reserve-up costs of ~$20–$40/day appear materially higher than efficient-market levels. The high costs stem from five key market design choices: 15-minute dispatch requirement, 30-minute ramp limits, 0.85 attenuation factor on storage energy usage, tying storage state-of-charge to reserve schedules (disconnected from real-time RTD dispatch), and the reserve procurement level and demand-curve shape. These design features inflate thermal commitment costs and create high opportunity costs for storage, making both thermal and storage sources expensive providers of imbalance reserves. Harvey notes some costs may be simulation artifacts (low storage energy offer prices, high reserve offer prices, constraint modeling differences), but warns the high prices may accurately reflect actual EDAM design if storage energy usage must be tied to reserve schedules. The analysis does not recommend specific changes but flags the disconnect between high reserve prices and relatively low energy prices as requiring investigation before market launch.

Harvey notes that loopflows—inter-balancing-area power transfers that create congestion on parallel constraints—can significantly impact market efficiency and proposes moving toward a long-run financial-congestion-hedge design (akin to PJM/MISO firm-flow entitlements and joint congestion management) that decouples rent allocation from self-schedule requirements. An interim step would assign internal-constraint congestion rents to balancing areas based on flow entitlements rather than self-scheduling. This is relevant to hydro because reservoir and pumped-storage hydro participating in EDAM would face distorted dispatch incentives under the current self-schedule-based rebate structure, particularly in scenarios with large new loads (data centers) and remote renewable generation; loopflow-impact allocation also affects the transmission value and export economics of hydro-rich regions like the Northwest. stakeholders: Scott Harvey (California ISO, Market Surveillance Committee)
ai_summary: Scott Harvey (CAISO Market Surveillance Committee member) presents critical analysis of CAISO's August 22, 2025 straw proposal on market power mitigation, arguing that the ISO has not demonstrated non-competitive outcomes in recent years and that proposed system-level market-power tests applied to constrained regions lack evidence of actual withholding. Harvey contends that counterfactual simulations conflate volatile gas-cost methodology (understated gas input prices) with genuine market power and that applying mitigation to constrained-down regions is unwarranted. He separately explains conduct-and-impact test mechanics, noting that CAISO's competitive-LMP approach caps offers to default energy bids even when a resource's output would have zero price impact — a key distinction for batteries and pondage hydro. The presentation does not state a formal recommendation or next step, but signals Harvey's view that CAISO should require empirical proof of withholding days and accurate cost bases before expanding mitigation design. title: Presentation - Price Formation Enhancements - Market Surveillance Committee - Jan 16, 2026
relevance_reason: CAISO is redesigning BAA-level market power mitigation (affecting mitigation of storage and use-limited hydro offers) and advancing scarcity pricing — two mechanisms that directly shape hydro revenue through default energy bids, opportunity-cost offer treatment, and energy price formation during tight supply.
stakeholders: Joint LSEs (SCE on behalf of IOUs, POUs, and Six Cities) (Southern California Edison and Joint CA Load-Serving Entities); Vitol (Vitol); WPTF (Gridwell Consulting) (Western Power Trading Forum / Gridwell Consulting)
ai_summary: CAISO is pursuing two parallel tracks in its Price Formation Enhancements initiative. Track 1 advances BAA-level market power mitigation (BAAMPM) by incorporating load-serving obligations (LSO) into the competitiveness test, mitigating only net-pivotal suppliers rather than all suppliers in a failed BAA group, and formalizing a grouping algorithm that includes the CAISO BA itself. This refinement directly affects how CAISO identifies whether hydro and storage operators have market power and thus whether their offers face mitigation — the LSO adjustment should reduce false positives by exempting capacity genuinely needed to serve an affiliate's retail load. Track 2 defers comprehensive scarcity pricing redesign, with CAISO planning incremental improvements (ensuring scarcity prices when load is shed, enhancing pricing when load is 'armed') before undertaking more expansive work; the Joint LSEs (SCE on behalf of IOUs, POUs, and Six Cities) oppose Track 2, while the Western Power Trading Forum urges full development of an energy supply margin framework. The LSO proposal has outstanding design questions for WEIM-only BAAs on handling merchant affiliate allocation. Most exposed are pumped-storage operators and large reservoir hydro with significant market power footprints in multi-affiliate BAAs, and any hydro owner relying on opportunity-cost mitigation exemptions; the competitiveness test changes could tighten or relax mitigation exposure depending on how LSO allocation evolves in stakeholder discussion.

title: Presentation - Price Formation Issues - Market Surveillance Committee - Jan 16, 2026
relevance_reason: CAISO Market Surveillance Committee presentation on price-formation issues and reserve-product design directly affects hydropower revenue through scarcity-pricing mechanisms, reserve-procurement rules, and co-optimization of reserves with energy—all core inputs to hydro dispatch value and ancillary-service compensation.
stakeholders: Scott Harvey (California ISO / Western EIM Market Surveillance Committee)
ai_summary: Scott Harvey, CAISO Market Surveillance Committee member, presents two critical price-formation issues for the California ISO balancing area: (1) real-time price signals in stressed conditions (August 2020 case study shows low real-time prices failed to incent import supply despite high day-ahead prices, and current rules cap prices at $1,000 during non-spinning-reserve dispatch, understating shortage value to suppliers and consumers); and (2) absence of explicit 30- or 60-minute reserve products, forcing CAISO to procure thousands of MWs of buffer capacity via expensive load-conformance purchases (energy bought in FMM and settled at RTD imbalance prices, with costs varying wildly). Harvey recommends CAISO adopt a tiered reserve product with graduated demand-curve pricing (referencing NYISO's 10-step design: $0–$750 depending on shortage MW), co-optimized with energy, but cautions that existing flexiramp and imbalance-reserve implementation flaws (battery state-of-charge accounting, nodal-delivery tests, locational modeling) must be fixed first—work that will take years. Hydropower operators (especially pumped storage and flexible dispatchable units) are directly affected: better-designed reserve markets with co-optimization and scarcity-responsive pricing would raise the value of fast-response capacity and reduce reliance on out-of-market load conformance, increasing revenue certainty and reducing demand-side rationing risk.

title: Presentation - Scarcity Pricing - Market Surveillance Committee - Jan 16, 2026
relevance_reason: Scarcity pricing mechanisms directly affect hydro and storage revenue through energy price formation and penalty-value settings that influence investment signals and intra-day dispatch incentives.
ai_summary: James Bushnell (CAISO Market Surveillance Committee) presents an analysis of scarcity-pricing approaches in CAISO's pricing-enhancements initiative, arguing that penalty-value reassessment is more straightforward than adding new reserve products. The power-balance constraint (PBC) penalty currently stands at $1,000/MWh ($2,000 during 831-trigger conditions) and has remained unchanged for decades; at 2010 value it would equate to roughly $1,500 today. Bushnell argues that higher penalty values would strengthen incentives for storage resources to retain energy for scarce conditions, incentivize delivery of scheduled imports, and improve EDAM's ability to compete for scarce import MWh during tight western conditions. His recommendation is that penalty values be raised and coordinated across markets, potentially stepped up over time once a schedule is agreed, and that major new reserve products should await live EDAM experience. The implication: PSH and conventional hydro with storage capability would face stronger economic incentives to withhold energy for peak scarcity, increasing real-time dispatch revenue during tight periods but potentially affecting energy-market pricing dynamics in both day-ahead and real-time.

ai_summary: CAISO's Market Performance and Advanced Analytics team presented updated analysis of eight algorithm variants for the BAA-MPM test, evaluated on Q3 2025 data (July–September). The variants combine three design factors: adjusted grouping logic, addition of a Load Serving Obligation (LSO) component to the Residual Supply Index calculation, and testing CAISO as a balancing-area entity. Adding the LSO component materially increased pass rates across most balancing areas, particularly in import-constrained midday hours in the Pacific Northwest and Central/Mountain regions (PSEI, SCL, TPWR saw +19–21% improvements), while testing CAISO reduced pass rates for several BAAs in peak evening hours (19–21). ai_summary: The Planning Working Group reviewed PGRR 147 (Allowable Non-Consequential Load Loss Alignment), sponsored by Rayburn County Electric Cooperative, which proposes to expand ERCOT's allowance for non-consequential load loss in transmission planning. LCRA opposed the proposal, arguing that relaxed load-loss criteria could shift planning toward customer interruption as a reliability solution rather than transmission investment. ERCOT Operations agreed, noting that NERC requirements are minimum standards and ERCOT maintains stricter N-1-1 criteria to prevent non-consequential load loss during routine transmission outages. Rayburn and Oncor proposed a narrower approach limited to contractually interruptible customers on dedicated facilities, using predefined operational measures as an interim bridge pending long-term transmission upgrades. ERCOT Operations cautioned that widespread use of curtailment procedures for new large loads could be difficult to manage and blur the planning-operations boundary. Participants raised questions about contractual enforceability and quantification of costs under current criteria. The PGRR was tabled pending further language proposals from Rayburn, Oncor, and other stakeholders.

ai_summary: ERCOT's Alternate Baseline Test (ABT) Concept Paper describes a two-step process for assigning baselines to ERS Loads. Step 1 evaluates resources against five default baseline methods (M810, MDP, REG, MBMA, NEAR20); a method passes if P95 is 20% or less and absolute bias is 5% or less. Step 2 applies ABT only to resources failing all five defaults. ABT compares actual load against a reference load calculated from the 10 most recent qualifying same-day-type, non-price historical intervals at the same time of day; an interval is counted as reduced when actual load is at or below 50% of reference load. A resource fails ABT only when the high-price reduction rate exceeds 50% AND the non-price reduction rate is below 20%. The final baseline becomes the single approved baseline used for ERS offers and performance analysis.
