title: BAL-001-TRE-2 Process
relevance_reason: ERCOT's primary frequency response (PFR) evaluation and performance-scoring process for generating units directly parallels hydro's obligations in NERC BAL-001-TRE; this document details compliance mechanics, performance thresholds, and exclusion processes that would apply to any dispatchable hydro or PSH in ERCOT, and serves as a cross-market reference for how frequency response rules are operationalized.
ai_summary: ERCOT's BAL-001-TRE evaluation process establishes a rolling 12-month performance scorecard for all generating units' primary frequency response during Frequency Measurable Events (FMEs). Resources must maintain a rolling average PFR score of 0.75 or above; those failing to meet this threshold or scoring below 0.75 for three consecutive FMEs become subject to reduction in their Ramping Reserve Service (RRS) MW allocation based on past performance. Market participants have 30 days from MIS posting to request exclusions for legitimate operating conditions that impaired normal PFR performance; ERCOT makes final determinations, though the PDCWG may be asked to advise. This scheme links frequency-response performance directly to reserve-service capability — a dispatchable resource's ability to provide RRS is capped by its demonstrated PFR capability during disturbances, creating a performance-based ratchet on flexibility services.

The ISO presented transition mechanics for resource accreditation (moving from Qualified Capacity to Marginal Reliability Impact Capacity or MRIC), covering a proposed two-year glide path using weighted averages of current and seasonal MRIC values; a post-modeling adjustment to boost energy-limited and storage resource accreditation by approximately 18% in winter to correct for Reserve Adequacy Assessment model limitations; and proposed Capacity Internal Bilateral Transactions (Capacity IBTs) as a new price-hedging instrument to address the shift from 40-month forward auctions to seasonal auctions one month ahead. Stakeholders including FirstLight Power and Advanced Energy United offered alternative load-weighting methodologies claiming the ISO's optimized weather-year sampling understates multi-day winter events critical to storage and energy-limited resource modeling. The Committee flagged concerns that seasonal accreditation differences could produce materially different revenue impacts across resource types, that modeling at "at-criteria" rather than expected system conditions may misalign market procurement, and that the adjustment for energy-limited resources lacks permanent modeling fixes. The ISO stated it does not currently propose to model all 70 years of winter hourly loads, intends no delay of core auction timing or deactivation changes, and acknowledged it would provide additional impact analysis, tariff redlines, and technical engagement on multi-day event representation.
hydro_read_through: This document does not name hydropower or pumped storage explicitly, but energy-limited and storage resources are a central topic. The accreditation methodology and the 18% winter adjustment apply to any resource with multi-hour duration and energy limitations, including pumped-storage hydro and run-of-river generators during high-flow seasons. The stakes are direct: the weighting of historical weather years, the model's treatment of multi-day charging windows, the baseline MRIC calculation, and the final adjustment formula will set the seasonal capacity prices (MRIC values) on which PSH and energy-limited hydro depend for seasonal revenue. Stakeholder pushback on the ISO's load-weighting approach suggests the current proposal may undervalue storage and energy-limited resources relative to firm resources, which could depress PSH capacity accreditation and hence clearing prices. If the ISO's methodology is adopted unchanged, owners of PSH and long-duration hydro facilities should expect lower seasonal-accreditation values than competitors whose input-cost structures align better with the model's assumptions about multi-day event frequency.

ai_summary: ISO-NE presented preliminary design for Capacity Auction Reforms – Seasonal Accreditation (CAR-SA), a major capacity market restructuring moving from annual auctions to seasonal (summer/winter) auctions and replacing annual Qualified Capacity (QC) accreditation with seasonal Marginal Reliability Impact Capacity (MRIC) values. Key elements include: (1) a proposed two-year transition allowing resources to sell weighted-average of current QC and seasonal MRIC values; (2) resource accreditation modeling using optimized subsets of 70-year weather data; (3) a post-modeling adjustment increasing accreditation for energy-limited and storage resources (approximately 18% winter adjustment) to address Reserve Adequacy Assessment model limitations in charging representation; (4) deactivation mitigation redlines conforming existing rules to seasonal MRIC framework; (5) seller-side offer mitigation including Capacity Offer Price Threshold (COPT) methodology estimated at approximately $5/kW-month; (6) buyer-side mitigation floors and recalculation procedures; (7) Capacity Internal Bilateral Transactions (Capacity IBTs) for price hedging using floating seasonal clearing prices. Committee raised extensive concerns about weather-year weighting potentially overstating multi-day winter events affecting storage accreditation, modeling of energy-limited resource charging and duration assumptions, at-criteria versus expected-conditions assumptions, and transparency of transition mechanics and demand-curve changes. FirstLight Power and Flatiron Energy presented alternative load-weighting methodologies and risk-modeling approaches; Advanced Energy United proposed weather-year weighting refinements and intertie modeling changes. The ISO indicated it would consider technical engagement on multi-day event representation and would provide additional detail on transition formulas, COPT derivation, and seasonal offer construction in July. Next steps include further stakeholder engagement on accreditation modeling, transition mechanics, and Tariff redlines.
hydro_read_through: This document addresses the single largest change to hydro revenue recognition in ISO-NE's capacity market: the move from annual Qualified Capacity to seasonal MRIC accreditation, which will establish how much seasonal capacity each hydro and pumped-storage facility can offer and be paid for. The proposed transition mechanism (weighted average of QC and seasonal MRIC for two years) affects investment certainty during the changeover. The 18% winter adjustment for energy-limited resources is critical to pumped-storage accreditation, as the base MRIC methodology may understate PSH's reliability contribution by failing to model storage charging from other generators during stressed hours. The weather-year weighting and at-criteria modeling choices will materially affect both the seasonality of accreditation values and their absolute levels — stakeholders representing storage interests are flagging that the ISO's current approach may overstate winter scarcity duration, artificially boosting winter accreditation but misaligning market signals with actual resource-constrained periods. Offer mitigation rules (COPT at ~$5/kW-month, cost-based opportunity-cost testing) will govern whether hydro owners can clear their true economic value or be forced to offer below avoidable cost. The seasonal design will also create new hedging needs (Capacity IBTs) for resources whose value now depends on highly variable seasonal prices rather than a single annual clearing price. Directness: these are not general market changes; they are hydro's accreditation and revenue framework for the coming decade.

relevance_reason: MECHANISM: This memo directly addresses offer formulation rules for ISO-NE's Capacity Auction and Resource (CAR) market, which determines how resources—including hydropower and pumped-storage facilities—calculate and submit capacity bids; the rules govern the cost basis (incremental costs, opportunity costs from Pay for Performance, annual-cost allocation) that hydro operators must use to stay competitive and avoid mitigation challenges, and it explicitly addresses the interaction between offer formulation and market-power mitigation thresholds.
initiatives: Capacity Auction Reforms [Active]
ai_summary: ISO-NE has issued a detailed guidance memo on how Capacity Resources should formulate competitive offers under the CAR-SA (Seasonal Accreditation) framework. The memo teaches that a competitive offer must equal the resource's expected incremental cost of accepting a Capacity Supply Obligation, including the opportunity cost of the PfP (Pay for Performance) scarcity-condition obligation and the cost of any annual-basis expenses allocated across seasonal offerings. The guidance explicitly advises market participants to consult the Internal Market Monitor (IMM) before submitting offers that may exceed the Capacity Offer Price Threshold or involve resource-specific concerns such as risk modeling or annual-cost treatment; the IMM cannot direct offer prices but can validate cost assumptions and whether expectations are reasonably justified. This creates a new compliance pathway for hydro and PSH owners in ISO-NE: operators allocating multi-year capex or seasonal energy availability into capacity-offer costs will need to pre-clear their methodology with the IMM to avoid triggering mitigation and price caps. The memo is comprehensive reference material (no vote or deadline stated) suitable for long-term corpus use by NHA members evaluating ISO-NE's cost-substantiation regime.

title: 2026-07-16 TC A03 ISO-NE Surplus Interconnection Service Gap Analysis, Part 1 – Interconnection
relevance_reason: MECHANISM: Surplus interconnection service rules directly affect hydro owners' ability to co-locate new generation (including pumped storage) at existing hydropower sites without triggering full interconnection studies, reducing development cost and timeline for uprates and repowering — a key strategic option for extending asset life and revenue.
ai_summary: ISO-NE is analyzing gaps in its Surplus Interconnection Service rules (Schedule 22/23 OATT) to streamline co-location of new resources at existing generator sites. The analysis follows NEPOOL's 2025 priority request and builds on FERC Order 2023 compliance filings (May 2024, accepted by FERC in 2025) that allowed surplus service to be used immediately upon interconnection agreement execution. Part 1 identifies rule gaps; Part 2 (separate document) addresses market participation models for co-located resources. Current rules limit surplus service to affiliates or third parties with original customer consent, exclude retiring/repowering facilities, and require commercial operation status for CNR (capacity) service. Hydro owners considering uprates, pumped-storage additions, or hybrid development at existing sites should review stakeholder discussions at NEPOOL Transmission Committee and watch for gap-analysis conclusions and proposed tariff solutions, which will shape interconnection timelines and costs for co-located projects.

title: 2026-07-16 TC A03 ISO-NE Surplus Interconnection Service Gap Analysis, Part 2 – Market Participation and Operational Considerations
relevance_reason: Surplus interconnection service rules directly affect hydropower uprates and co-location revenue options; the document clarifies market participation models (Generator Asset/Capacity Resource constructs) and energy/ancillary service obligations for multiple facilities behind a single point of interconnection—a canonical use case for small hydro expansion and pumped-storage facilities.
ai_summary: ISO-NE released Part 2 of its Surplus Interconnection Service Gap Analysis, clarifying market participation rules for multiple generating facilities co-located behind a single interconnection point, including those using surplus capacity from existing hydro or PSH plants. The document specifies four configuration options (separate or single Generator Assets paired with separate or single Capacity Resources) and maps which Lead Market Participant responsibility applies to each: single-asset constructs consolidate offer submission and dispatch under one participant (reducing autonomy but simplifying coordination), while separate-asset constructs allow each facility independent participation but require multiple participants to coordinate compliance with shared Interconnection Service limits. This guidance is critical for hydro owners considering uprates, pumped-storage co-location, or use-limited resource expansion, since interconnection service constraints will likely force facility-limitation configurations; the document also flags a technical complication with single-asset structures if the original interconnection customer's facility deactivates, which could jeopardize the subordinate surplus resource.

title: 2026-07-16 TC A03 Surplus Interconnection Service Gap Analysis Presentation
relevance_reason: Surplus Interconnection Service rules directly affect how hydropower and pumped-storage facilities can add resources, repower, or co-locate at existing interconnection points without triggering new cluster studies — a material option for uprating and hybrid/co-located resource deployment.
ai_summary: ISO-NE's Surplus Interconnection Service Gap Analysis (posted July 10, 2026) proposes five interconnection reforms: a new expedited process for additions, replacements, and modifications at existing POIs that don't increase service or require network upgrades; revised definition of Unused Capability to support CNRIS sharing and hybrid-resource accreditation; explicit clarification that energy-storage facilities can be surplus interconnection customers when charging from the grid; public posting of surplus-service requests; and timelines and procedural detail for surplus studies. The analysis also documents market-participation registration options (separate vs. combined generator assets and capacity resources) for surplus and original facilities co-located behind the same POI. Most consequential for hydro owners is the expedited pathway for co-located additions and facility replacements — currently only available through subordinate Surplus Interconnection Service status — which would allow original-level service and alignment with CAR-SA hybrid-resource accreditation rules being developed in parallel. Next steps include stakeholder review and ISO development of specific tariff language; no vote date is stated in this presentation.

title: 2026-07-16 TC A04.1 New England Large & Co-Located Loads Show Cause Order (EL26-72) Compliance: Abeyance Request & Section 205 Filing

stakeholders: Alex Rost (ISO New England); Nic Baldenko (ISO New England); TC Secretary (ISO New England); NEPOOL Counsel (NEPOOL)
ai_summary: FERC issued a Section 206 order on June 18, 2026 (EL26-72) finding ISO-NE's tariff unjust and unreasonable for lack of large and co-located load integration provisions. ISO-NE and the PTOs plan to file a 90-day abeyance request by August 3, 2026, followed by a Section 205 tariff filing on November 16, 2026, addressing five reform categories: efficient study processes, cost transparency, co-location rules (including behind-the-meter generation definitions and netting restrictions), flexible load services (interim RNS, firm and non-firm contract demand services), and generation studies for electrically proximate loads. Hydro and PSH owners should monitor the tariff design details—particularly the BTMG netting rules and flexible service definitions—because these directly constrain or enable co-location and behind-the-meter hydropower arrangements in New England. The stakeholder schedule runs through November 12, 2026 (Participants Committee vote), with TC briefings on August 18–19, Markets Committee and TC reviews in September, and votes in October–November.

title: 2026-07-16 TC A04.2 New England Large & Co-Located Loads Show Cause Order (EL26-72) Compliance: Informational Report on Resource Adequacy
relevance_reason: Large-load growth and co-located load interconnection directly expand the addressable market for hydro's energy and flexibility products, while capacity-market and energy-price signals discussed here determine hydro's revenue sustainability and new-entry incentives.
stakeholders: Al McBride (ISO New England Inc.); Gordon van Welie (ISO New England Inc.)
ai_summary: ISO-NE filed a FERC compliance report (EL26-72) on resource adequacy for large loads (particularly data centers) entering New England. The report affirms that existing competitive energy and capacity markets are well-positioned to attract new supply and retain the existing fleet, citing forward energy prices currently near or at cost-of-entry for new generation. ISO-NE describes several market-refinement projects underway: reductions to the Pay-for-Performance penalty rate (which disproportionately burdens slow-start resources), Capacity Auction Reforms affecting accreditation methodology, improvements to Surplus Interconnection Service, probabilistic forecasting, and uncertainty reserves. For hydro owners, the key mechanics are (1) large-load growth will tighten energy markets and raise scarcity pricing, especially in winter when data centers compete with heating load; (2) co-location rules and interconnection protocols being developed will determine whether hydro can serve load behind-the-meter or tap surplus interconnection at existing plants; (3) PFP rate reduction and CONE updates directly affect the capacity revenues hydro operators depend on for fleet retention; and (4) probabilistic forecasting and uncertainty reserves may create new ramping/flexibility product opportunities. The report signals ISO-NE's expectation of tariff amendments to facilitate large-load entry and expects these changes to be completed within the ongoing stakeholder process.

ai_summary: ISO-NE Manual RPA (Registration and Performance Auditing) Revision 22, effective November 1, 2026, incorporates Order 2222 conforming changes governing registration of Distributed Energy Resource Aggregations (DERAs), DERs, and alternative technologies. The manual establishes that a DERA must have a single Lead Market Participant (the DER Aggregator) responsible for registering aggregations under one or more participation models, assigning Demand Designated Entities, mapping resources to dispatch locations, and ensuring compliance with all ISO asset requirements. DERs within a DERA cannot transfer between aggregations and must be retired and re-registered to move; the DDE is responsible for RTU installation and mapping DRRs/DRDERAs to remote terminal units. This framework creates new participation pathways for small hydropower and distributed storage but also imposes strict aggregation governance, single-point-of-control dispatch requirements, and metering/telemetry standards that could increase compliance costs for small-to-mid-size hydro operators entering aggregation structures.

title: 2026-07-07-09 MC A03a - CAR-SA: Proposal Overview - Presentation
relevance_reason: MECHANISM: ISO-NE's Capacity Auction Reforms (CAR-SA) restructure capacity accreditation and seasonal procurement to reflect resource-specific reliability contributions, directly affecting how hydro and pumped-storage accreditation values are calculated and the seasonal demand curves that set their capacity revenue.
initiatives: Capacity Auction Reforms [Active]; Order No. 2222 [Active]
ai_summary: ISO-NE proposes moving from annual to seasonal (summer/winter) capacity auctions with accreditation reforms tied to Expected Unserved Energy (EUE) reduction, effective Q2 2027. The design improves resource operational-characteristic modeling—including energy-limited and storage resources—and calculates accreditation values (rMRI) based on margro reliability impact at system-adequacy criteria, rather than uniform assumptions. This revalues hydro and pumped-storage capacity by season and by performance characteristics (outage rates, generation profiles, energy limits); a transition mechanism will phase in the new rules. Key implications for storage and energy-limited hydro: accreditation will reflect their seasonal and state-dependent contributions more precisely, affecting revenue in capacity auctions and long-term investment signals. FERC accepted the prior CAR-PD filing in March 2026; CAR-SA filing anticipated by end of 2026, with key auction activities in first half of 2027.

title: 2026-07-07-09 MC A03b - CAR-SA: Transition Mechanism, cont. - Presentation
relevance_reason: CAR-SA's seasonal capacity accreditation and marginal reliability impact (MRIC) methodology directly reshapes how hydro (especially pumped storage and seasonal resources) is credited in ISO-NE's capacity market, altering revenue recognition across seasons and affecting reserve margins that determine must-offer and procurement rules.
initiatives: Capacity Auction Reforms [Active]; Order No. 2222 [Active]
ai_summary: ISO-NE is implementing Capacity Auction Reforms – Seasonal/Accreditation (CAR-SA) with a three-year transition beginning in CCP 2028–29 (Q2 2027 proposed effective date). The reform shifts accreditation from a long-standing annual Qualified Capacity (QC) methodology to seasonal Marginal Reliability Impact Capacity (MRIC) values that reflect resource contributions to each season's adequacy. During transition, each resource's accredited capacity will be a weighted average: Year 1 (2/3 QC + 1/3 MRIC), Year 2 (1/3 QC + 2/3 MRIC), Year 3 (full MRIC). Hydro owners—particularly seasonal resources like winter-peaking or pumped-storage operators—will experience year-by-year accreditation shifts; some resources (e.g. passive demand response and winter solar) will see accreditation rise under CAR-SA, while others (especially summer-peaking hydro) will experience lower recognized capacity. The demand curve for procurement will also shift leftward across the three-year glide path, mirroring supply-side accreditation changes to maintain unit consistency and cost equivalence. Next steps include stakeholder review of transition mechanics and expected board/Markets Committee approval in coming meetings.

title: 2026-07-07-09 MC A03c - CAR-SA: Updated Activity Schedule - Presentation

The activity schedule governs the timing of resource qualification, market-power mitigation reviews, demand-curve development, and auction windows — all of which directly affect how hydro resources are accredited, how their capacity offers are mitigated, and when they must submit data. Most relevant to pumped-storage and seasonal-constraint hydro: the seasonal framework, the integration of accreditation into RA modeling, the Installed Capacity Requirement process, and the qualification deadlines (resource-qualification data submission one month pre-auction; unexpected full forced outage window tied to seller-side market power close). The presentation is an activity-schedule roadmap with no votes or comment deadlines stated; follow-up questions may be submitted in writing to Jasleen Singh by July 27, 2026, and this is Phase 2 of the CAR workstream, with Final Design and tariff amendments scheduled for Q4 2026.

title: 2026-07-07-09 MC A03d - CAR-SA: Storage and Energy-Limited Resource Modeling and Accreditation Design Updates Cont. - Presentation
relevance_reason: CAPACITY ACCREDITATION: ISO-NE is updating how pumped-storage and energy-limited resources are credited toward resource adequacy; the rMRI adjustment mechanism directly affects the capacity value (MRIC) PSH owners receive in the ISO-NE capacity auction.
initiatives: Capacity Auction Reforms [Active]; Order No. 2222 [Active]
ai_summary: ISO-NE proposes an upward rMRI adjustment for energy-limited and storage resources in its Capacity Auction Reforms: Seasonal/Accreditation (CAR-SA) initiative, effective Q2 2027. The adjustment corrects a MARS modeling limitation that prevents storage from charging other storage during constrained hours, which currently underestimates storage reliability value. The formula scales adjusted rMRI so that very long-duration storage with zero forced outage rate would receive an rMRI of 1 (fully available). For a 10-hour battery, the winter adjustment increases rMRI from 0.414 to 0.492; for a 12-hour energy-limited resource, summer rMRI increases from 0.839 to 0.851. Class-level impacts show winter MRIC gains of 149.9 MW for energy storage and 140.0 MW for oil/dual-fuel, with larger adjustments favoring longer-duration resources. title: 2026-07-07-09 MC A03f - CAR-SA: FirstLight Power - Presentation
relevance_reason: ISO-NE's CAR-SA capacity accreditation design—particularly seasonal payment-rate allocation, MRI-based CONE splits, and at-criteria accreditation—directly affects how pumped-storage hydro and seasonal hydro resources are compensated and incentivized to enter, especially when supply is tight in only one season.
initiatives: Capacity Auction Reforms [Active]; Order No. 2222 [Active]
ai_summary: FirstLight Power presents technical analysis of interconnected design flaws in ISO-NE's Capacity Accreditation and Reserves-Seasonal Attributes (CAR-SA) proposal to the Markets Committee. The core issue: the current design allocates seasonal capacity payment rates proportional to Marginal Reliability Index (MRI) at Net ICR for each season, driven by an administrative 50/50 seasonal risk split, weather-year weighting that overstates winter event duration, and accreditation at 'at-criteria' conditions (demand-curve location inconsistent with actual clearing risk). FirstLight demonstrates that under this design, a reference resource may not recover Net CONE annually even when the system is tight in one season, suppressing entry signals for seasonal capacity. Potential solutions offered include dynamic seasonal risk splits aligned to actual system conditions, accreditation within a feasible clearing-point range, revised weather-year weighting, and payment-rate approaches that ensure annual Net CONE recovery. No deadline or vote date specified; this is positioned as urgent discussion to prevent compounding design errors before CAR-SA implementation. Pumped-storage operators—particularly those operating in winter-constrained regions or managing seasonal energy constraints—face material revenue exposure: if winter accreditation and payment rates are structurally overstated relative to summer, then summer-constrained capacity and flexibility are undervalued, and winter-heavy PSH assets may receive artificially elevated seasonal payments that don't reflect true entry incentives.

title: 2026-07-07-09 MC A03g - CAR-SA: Flatiron Feedback, cont. - Presentation
relevance_reason: CAPACITY/RA accreditation methodology — proposal to reshape how ISO-NE models marginal resource adequacy contributions (rMRI) for all resources including hydro, affecting accreditation values, capacity-market clearing prices, and revenue recovery for dispatchable and storage units under ISO-NE's Competitive Auctions with Reserves (CAR) framework.
initiatives: Capacity Auction Reforms [Active]; Order No. 2222 [Active]
ai_summary: Flatiron Energy presents a critique of ISO-NE's proposed Capacity Accreditation and Reserves (CAR-SA) modeling assumptions, arguing that the 'accreditation base case' (which adds 5 GW of load and uses historical 2002–03 extreme-weather years) creates artificially long marginal resource index (MRI) events that over-accredit resources designed for conditions that won't materialize. Flatiron proposes an 'Expected System Conditions' pathway: modeling expected supply and forecasted load without artificial load scaling, which would reduce or eliminate simulated MRI hours in a system with excess capacity. When MRI hours are minimal, Flatiron proposes accreditation shift to MRIC (marginal resource index credit) based on EFORd (equivalent forced outage rate) for most resource types, reflecting contingency-driven rather than energy-shortage-driven reliability events. ISO-NE's capacity demand curve and Net ICR would adjust accordingly, but the price-formation mechanism (reference-unit recovery at Net CONE × rMRI factor) would be preserved. This proposal, if adopted, would fundamentally change how all accredited resources including hydro, pumped storage, and thermal units recover capacity value, with most exposure to resource types whose value depends heavily on modeled energy availability in GE MARS software.

ai_summary: Advanced Energy United presents three conceptual amendments to ISO-NE's Capacity Accreditation Reforms (CAR-SA): (1) replace peak-day weather-year weighting with multi-day event metrics to avoid overstating winter cold-snap frequency and undervaluing storage; (2) model intertie import profiles hourly rather than as flat capacity blocks to reflect overnight export availability when storage would charge; (3) reclassify storage resources as EL3 (energy-limited, fully rechargeable daily) rather than Type 3 to address systemic understatement of off-peak charging energy and state-of-charge modeling gaps. These amendments target the root cause that CAR-SA's accreditation model understates storage's realistic value and charging opportunities, thereby depressing investment signals for flexible resources that ISO-NE needs for seasonal adequacy and decarbonization. title: 2026-07-07-09 MC A03k - CAR-SA: Tariff Redlines - Auditing - Presentation

ai_summary: ISO-NE proposes to sunset existing Claimed Capability and Seasonal DR audits after August 31, 2027, replacing them with three new metrics: Global Maximum Capability (36-month rolling max hourly performance, updated weekly), Seasonal Maximum Capability (same but for seasonally-specific temperature conditions), and Seasonal Dependable Capability (median availability during the 100 highest load hours per season, with a performance factor applied to dispatchable resources). The framework treats dispatchable resources (those receiving electronic dispatch instructions) differently from non-dispatchable resources, applying a performance factor to dispatchable median offers. This is part of ISO-NE's broader Capacity Auction Reforms (CAR-SA) initiative scheduled for Q2 2027 implementation. Most exposed are conventional hydropower operators, especially dispatchable hydro in ISO-NE's system, whose seasonal dependable credits will now hinge on demonstrated performance during peak-load hours rather than on-demand auditing — reducing discretion to claim seasonal uplifts and tying accreditation to actual dispatch compliance and offer discipline.

title: 2026-07-07-09 MC A03l - CAR-SA: Winter Gas Constraint, cont. - Presentation
relevance_reason: The proposal establishes a non-firm gas capacity demand curve and bilateral-transaction rules affecting how gas-backed resources—and by extension, competing dispatchable and storage resources—are accredited and compensated in ISO-NE's capacity market, directly impacting hydro's competitive position and RA value.
initiatives: Capacity Auction Reforms [Active]; Order No. 2222 [Active]
ai_summary: ISO-NE's Capacity Auction Reforms (CAR-SA) introduce a non-firm gas capacity demand curve effective Q2 2027 to reflect winter regional gas-supply constraints in capacity-market pricing. The proposal specifies: (1) gas-contract requirements (16-hour daily firmness for LNG; affidavit requirements dropped); (2) bilateral CSO (Capacity Supply Obligation) transaction limits tied to truncation points on the demand curve, preventing overtrading of constrained non-firm capacity across zones; and (3) restrictions on gas-only resource-backed imports, which cannot sell non-firm CSO in winter. The mechanism directly affects hydro's accreditation and capacity revenue: by capping non-firm gas capacity and pricing it separately, ISO-NE reduces the volume of low-cost gas capacity competing in winter auctions, tightening supply and raising clearing prices for all resources—especially valuable for pumped-storage hydro and reservoir hydro with winter peaking capability. The filing to stakeholders occurred in July 2026; the ISO notes it will "assess potential enhancements... in the months to come and after the CAR-SA filing." Most exposed are PSH and winter-peaking conventional hydro in zonal export-constrained areas, which benefit from reduced gas competition in winter RA auctions.

The methodology explicitly excludes offshore wind from the replacement portfolio due to buildout uncertainty, leaving a net-generation gap in retirement scenarios that hydro supply could fill. ai_summary: ISO-NE has redlined Section II of its tariff to establish a formal Deactivation Notification process for permanent resource retirements, effective for the Capacity Commitment Period beginning June 1, 2028. Generators seeking to retire must file a deactivation notice by the first business day within 12 months of each CCP start; resources >20 MW are subject to a 90-day reliability review, after which ISO may delay deactivation if needed for local transmission reliability and offer net going-forward-cost compensation. Key mechanics: (1) resources that never held Capacity Network Resource Interconnection Service (CNR or equivalent) can deactivate by simple written notice; (2) resources inactive for three calendar years are deemed automatically deactivated unless repower-application protections apply; (3) Lead Market Participants must submit detailed cost workbooks and officer affidavits, subject to Internal Market Monitor audit. ai_summary: Massachusetts Attorney General's Office supports ISO-NE's proposed post-implementation adjustments to the Day-Ahead Ancillary Services (DA A/S) market, citing cost overruns in the market's first year (actual incremental cost $921–974 million vs. $140 million forecast). title: 2026-06-09-11 MC A03a - DA/AS Post-Implementation Adjustments - Presentation

ai_summary: ISO-NE proposes targeted adjustments to its day-ahead ancillary services (DA A/S) design, effective October 22, 2026, based on February 2026 Internal Market Monitor recommendations. The FER DQ reduction for variable wind/solar will also shift the composition of reliability-based demand, potentially favoring the fast-ramping and continuous-availability profile that hydro supplies. title: 2026-06-09-11 MC A04a - CAR-SA: Transition Mechanism Introduction - Presentation

ai_summary: ISO-NE proposes a Capacity Auction Reforms – Seasonal/Accreditation (CAR-SA) transition mechanism (target Q2 2027 effective date) that will gradually shift resource accreditation from current Qualified Capacity to proposed seasonal MRIC (Minimum Reliability Impact Contribution) values over two transition years (two summer and two winter seasons), with full phased design taking effect in Capacity Commitment Period 21. The transition uses a weighted-average approach: in Year 1, a 100 MW QC resource with 70 MW summer MRIC and 40 MW winter MRIC would be accredited at 90 MW (summer) and 80 MW (winter); by Year 3 it falls to the full MRIC floor (70/40 MW). Hydro owners will face material accreditation volatility during transition because MRIC values depend on seasonal performance during modeled Minimum Reliability Interest hours, potentially creating seasonal mismatches between what resources can offer and what demand curves procure. ISO-NE is still assessing demand-curve transition mechanics and whether to transition the winter gas constraint; comments and questions are due to Markets Committee Secretary Jasleen Singh (Jsingh@iso-ne.com) by June 24, 2026, with further stakeholder meetings scheduled through Q3 2026 before FERC filing.

title: 2026-06-09-11 MC A04b - CAR-SA: Resource Accreditation Modeling cont. - Presentation

initiatives: Capacity Auction Reforms [Active]; Order No. 2222 [Active]
ai_summary: ISO-NE is modeling accreditation outcomes under its proposed CAR-SA design using a 70-year weather-adjusted load dataset (weighted subset of years 2000/01–2022/23 for winter; 2007–2023 for summer) to capture long-term weather variability and peak-load scenarios. Sensitivity analysis shows that explicitly modeling all 70 years of winter hourly loads produces nearly identical net ICR, reliability metrics (LOLE, LOLH, EUE), and accreditation results (rMRI) across all resource types — including Daily/Weekly Hydro (96.1–96.2%), Energy Storage (20.9–21.7%), and IPR-Hydro (59.9–61.0%) — compared to the ISO's proposed weighted-year approach. The ISO assessed and rejected FirstLight Resource Management's alternate block-based weighting methodology, concluding it ignores inter-block weather correlations and temporal heterogeneity, understating the likelihood of severe winters and distorting the upper tail of the load distribution where resource adequacy is most critical. The proposed framework will remain in place for CAR-SA implementation targeting Q2 2027; FirstLight's alternative approach was a stakeholder submission rather than ISO proposal.

The adjustment is projected to be finalized Q4 2026 with FERC filing and Q2 2027 effective date. Stakeholders should submit feedback to Jasleen Singh (jsingh@iso-ne.com) by June 24, 2026. title: 2026-06-09-11 MC A04j - CAR-SA: Interactions with PFP - Presentation

initiatives: Capacity Auction Reforms [Active]; Order No. 2222 [Active]

ai_summary: ISO-NE presents three approaches to cap the Balancing Ratio (BR) under its seasonal capacity auction reform (CAR-SA), addressing a FERC order requiring the BR cap at 1.0 to prevent resources from being obligated beyond physical capability. The migration from Qualified Capacity to Marginal Reliability Impact (MRI) accreditation will reduce total capacity supply obligations system-wide, raising BRs and causing the 1.0 cap to bind more frequently, which shrinks Capacity Performance Payments (CPPs) to overperformers due to funding deficiencies. ISO-NE's preferred Approach 3 would cap the BR at a seasonal ratio tied to net maximum capability divided by net MRIC (1.355 in summer, 1.444 in winter), preserving stronger performance incentives for overperformance while complying with FERC's logic. Additionally, ISO-NE proposes conforming the annual PFP stop-loss limit to a seasonal market by capping seasonal losses at two times (instead of three times) a resource's maximum monthly net loss. Stakeholder feedback is due to Jasleen Singh (jsingh@iso-ne.com) by June 24, 2026, with ISO-NE targeting July for its final proposal. Large-duration and seasonal-flexibility resources (including pumped storage and multi-week-capable reservoirs) are most exposed, as their value in CAR-SA depends on accreditation during scarcity hours; how the BR cap settles will determine whether they receive full or reduced CPP rates during performance.

title: 2026-06-09-11 MC A04k - CAR-SA: Capacity Bilaterals - Presentation

ai_summary: ISO-NE proposes to implement Capacity Internal Bilateral Transactions (IBTs)—an ISO-administered financial instrument allowing participants to hedge capacity-market price risk by fixing capacity payments—and to simplify capacity-export rules under the seasonal Capacity Auction Reforms (CAR-SA), effective Q2 2027. Under CAR-SA, capacity clearing occurs ~1 month before each 6-month season (vs. 40+ months ahead under the old FCM), shortening the forward-price visibility window and raising hedging demand. The Capacity IBT would allow a supplier and LSE to exchange fixed-for-floating swaps on capacity obligations, with the ISO settling the floating leg (pegged to seasonal clearing prices or CLO charge rates) and netting it within ISO settlement, while the fixed leg stays off-ISO books. Separately, ISO-NE would discontinue rarely-used export-bid curtailment exemptions (III.1.10.7(f) and III.15.8.1.2) and consolidate export functionality under simpler rules (III.1.10.7(i)), allowing capacity exporters to submit opportunity costs that determine MRIC eligibility. Hydro and PSH operators using export strategies or managing capacity revenues through bilateral hedges will see changes to both pricing instruments and export curtailment priority; the proposal suggests March 2027 implementation and is under stakeholder feedback.

relevance_reason: MECHANISM: ISO-NE's Capacity Auction Reforms (CAR-SA) establish seasonal capacity-market offer formation rules and seller-side market power mitigation affecting how all resources, including hydropower and pumped storage, must construct and submit capacity bids, with direct implications for revenue recovery and mitigation risk.
initiatives: Capacity Auction Reforms [Active]; Order No. 2222 [Active]
ai_summary: ISO-NE presented seasonal offer construction methodology and seller-side market power mitigation rules for its Capacity Auction Reforms – Seasonal/Accreditation (CAR-SA) proceeding. The ISO proposes applying a Capacity Offer Price Threshold (COPT) methodology conformed from the FCA's Dynamic Delist Bid Threshold, capped at 25–75% of net Net CONE, plus a pivotal supplier test that automatically reduces bids above the threshold if the supplier is deemed pivotal. For the first seasonal auctions in CCP19, the ISO will use an initial COPT of 37% of annual Net CONE (derived from historical FCA16-18 ratios) rather than prior-auction pricing. The presentation illustrates offer formulation for generalized resources and gas-constrained resources by showing how next-best-alternative analysis drives capacity bids — resources whose NBA is temporary exit must cover netGFC plus expected PFP costs, while resources profitable in energy markets offer only the PFP common-value component. Hydro operators with seasonal revenue constraints (e.g., run-of-river or PSH facing winter/summer energy-market disparities) will need to validate whether their avoidable-cost calculations and PFP recovery assumptions survive the pivotal supplier test; if mitigated improperly, FERC cost-recovery procedures are available. Status and next steps are not stated in this presentation; the proceeding remains in detail-design phase.

title: 2026-06-09-11 MC A04n - CAR-SA: AEU Conceptual Amendments - Presentation
relevance_reason: ISO-NE's seasonal accreditation methodology directly affects how storage and flexible resources are valued in the capacity market, with specific proposals on weather-year weighting and intertie modeling that would alter the MRIC (Minimum Revenue Impacting Capacity) accreditation signal for pumped storage and other flexible resources.
initiatives: Capacity Auction Reforms [Active]; Order No. 2222 [Active]
ai_summary: Advanced Energy United presents two conceptual amendments to ISO-NE's seasonal accreditation reform (CAR-SA). Amendment 1 argues ISO's weather-year weighting based on peak-load days overstates the frequency of sustained cold snaps, causing storage (especially pumped storage) to be disproportionately penalized in accreditation; CAU proposes weighting years by the frequency of multi-day cold-weather blocks instead. Amendment 2 contends ISO's flat import-capacity block for intertie modeling obscures when actual imports are available (often overnight, between MRI hours), understating storage's charging opportunities and thus its MRIC value; CAU proposes modeling hourly import-availability profiles tied to load shape. The submission also flags a potential inconsistency between ISO-NE's use of LOLE for resource adequacy but EUE for accreditation, which could systematically undervalue storage. Storage accreditation is directly material to investment signals and RA sufficiency in New England; these amendments are being advanced in the context of ISO-NE's broader seasonal accreditation reform process.

ai_summary: PJM completed evaluation of 134 proposals (57 greenfields, 77 upgrades) submitted in its 2025 Reliability Window 1 and selected regional backbone solutions totaling ~$11.7 billion: a 222-mile 765 kV line from Kammer–Buttermilk–Juniata (Mid-Atlantic), a 185-mile 500 kV HVDC line from Heritage–Mosby (South/Dominion), and three 765/345 kV lines in PJM West (Greentown–Teddy–Marysville, Guernsey–Conesville–West Millersport–Adkins, and 345 kV laterals). ai_summary: Alliant Energy proposes Bridge Interim Transmission Service (BITS), a non-firm interim transmission product for large loads in MISO that allows service to begin once load interconnection studies are complete and local facilities are built, while required network upgrades are under construction—automatically converting to firm Network Integration Transmission Service (NITS) when upgrades finish. BITS requires load to have metering and telemetry in place, 24/7 contact availability, and ability to reduce load in 30 minutes if curtailed; loads are backed by accredited capacity resources and included in Module E forecasts. This removes a timing mismatch that has deterred large-load interconnection: hydro owners co-locating loads or offering behind-the-meter service can now ramp customers into service faster, capturing scarcity premiums from load growth without waiting years for transmission buildout. The proposal aligns with FERC's Large Load Show Cause Order (EL26-70) for MISO; Alliant seeks stakeholder feedback by August 7, 2026, and proposes FERC filing in Q4 2026 with implementation March 2027.

title: New Issue - Non Firm Large Load

MECHANISM: Non-firm load participation raises two direct concerns for hydro owners. Second, if non-firm loads ARE curtailed preferentially during scarcity events, hydro operators face reduced dispatch value in real-time scarcity periods, since the non-firm load absorbs the curtailment instead of pushing higher locational prices. MISO's design choices on RA treatment and curtailment-dispatch rules will determine whether non-firm loads are free-riders on hydro's scarcity value or are appropriately penalized. title: 20260709 MSC Item 12 Enhance Reserve Deliverability for DA and RT Market (MSC-2026-2).pdf

ai_summary: MISO staff presents an analysis of Regulation reserve clearing and performance deterioration: Regulation requirements roughly doubled on July 1, 2024 (to ~800 MW base), Regulation reserve prices rose 53% and mileage prices 71% year-over-year in 2025, yet non-performance penalties reached 31% of total Regulation revenue by 2025, with gas resource penalties rising more than 2x year-over-year. The document identifies that (1) Regulation performance is assessed only in settlement, after-the-fact, with no automated real-time feedback loop to disqualify poor performers (unlike offline Supplemental and STR); and (2) coal and gas performance has deteriorated while batteries have entered as significant Regulation suppliers. MISO staff indicate they are evaluating options to improve real-time clearing and performance monitoring, with next steps to follow. Pumped-storage operators should monitor this closely because: (i) rising Regulation prices increase PSH revenue exposure to that product, but (ii) potential automation of performance testing and real-time disqualification could advantage faster-ramping technologies (batteries) and penalize PSH and conventional hydro more heavily if response-time or consistency standards are tightened without accounting for hydro's multi-hour operational flexibility constraints.

ai_summary: MISO is evaluating updates to transmission constraint demand curves (TCDCs), which cap the shadow prices the market will pay to enforce network constraints, with particular focus on how undersized TCDCs interact with operating-reserve shortages to cause manual redispatches and Day-Ahead Marginal Assurance Payment (DAMAP) uplift. Dispatchable generators (including reservoir hydro) are most exposed: when reserves are scarce, high MEC penalties can force dispatch back to EcoMax despite binding constraints, then manual redispatch down creates the DAMAP liability. Hydro owners should track this work because enhanced TCDCs or dynamic reserve-shortage scaling could improve real-time economic dispatch and reduce the frequency of out-of-market corrections.

title: 20260709 MSC Item 13a DAMAP Reduction Total - New Issue Introduction (MSC-2026-7).pdf

Both changes require tariff filings; MSC-2026-7 has been introduced for adoption at the July 9, 2026 Market Subcommittee meeting. Any hydro or pumped-storage unit that experiences deratings, manual redispatch, or forced outages would receive more accurate (and typically higher) make-whole compensation under the corrected formulas.

Currently, the sum method can overstate total cleared MWs (since ancillary-service MWs can be shared with energy), leading to larger schedule reductions than physical capability warrants; the proposed method uses the maximum of two DART constraint combinations to more accurately cap the Reduction Total. Stakeholder feedback is due July 24, 2026, with a target Q3 2026 filing and 60-day effective date. title: 20260708 RASC Item 07 24 Hour Lead Time in Accreditation (RASC-2026-1).pdf

Solution 2 (zero availability for lead-time increases within 48 hours of the operating day) would penalize changes near emergencies but allow longer-lead resources to participate in multi-day FRAC. Solution 3 (sliding scale: full availability at 4 hours, declining 5% per hour to zero at 24+ hours) offers graduated incentives. MISO will select a recommended solution in August 2026, file revised tariff at FERC in October 2026. Stakeholders should comment by July 22, 2026. title: 20260629 LLWG Item 07 Large Load Interconnection Reliability Requirements (LLWG 2026 3)

ai_summary: MISO is filing revised Tariff language by end of July 2026 to impose interconnection reliability requirements on large loads (≥50 MW new, ≥25 MW cumulative increase) and computational loads (≥1 MW of data-center-type digital demand), implementing FERC's show-cause order. Requirements include basic facility data, modeling, hourly forecasts, telemetry, and PMU data; computational loads face additional phasor measurement, ride-through (voltage/frequency), and ramp-rate controls; MISO will install and charge customers for remote disconnect equipment and control systems. A transitional provision exempts loads with service commencement before 11/1/2027 from ramp and ride-through requirements for their lifetime unless they upgrade by ≥25 MW after 10/1/2026. This affects hydro owners because (1) it establishes a co-location precedent — large loads are now defined as discrete withdrawal points, creating opportunities for hydro to site behind-the-meter generation and enter direct load-service arrangements; (2) the ramp-rate and ride-through enforcement on computational loads (AI, crypto, HPC) creates a demand-side flexibility requirement that could be partially satisfied by hybrid hydro-storage systems and (3) the remote-disconnect and PMU mandates on loads set operational-control expectations that may extend to dispatchable generation. Stakeholders expressed concerns about applicability, transition, and specific language; feedback has influenced the revised Tariff language.

ai_summary: MISO proposes mandatory real-time SCADA telemetry (MW, MVAR, breaker status via ICCP) for all large loads and generation resources ≥20 MVA sharing the same point of interconnection, plus PMU installation (sampling at 60 Hz minimum in IEEE C37.118 format) at computational large loads before service commencement. Generation behind the large load's POI cannot be netted with load and must stream individual telemetry including state-of-charge data for battery or storage devices, and control-mode telemetry for market-participating generators. MISO requests feedback by July 13, 2026, with detailed requirements to be drafted in Business Practice Manuals. Pumped-storage facilities and conventional hydro units co-located at large-load sites (especially data-center campuses) will face new capital costs (PMU installation and ICCP comms) and operational constraints (non-netting, continuous dispatch visibility, reduced operational flexibility).

title: 20260629 LLWG Item 08b Large Load Operational Forecast Requirements (LLWG 2026 4A)

ai_summary: MISO proposes to require large loads (data centers, industrial facilities, campuses) to submit short-term operational forecasts at hourly (next 1–168 hours) and 5-minute (next 6 hours) granularities, feeding into MISO's Multi-Day/Next-Day/Intraday reliability commitment and look-ahead commitment/real-time dispatch processes. Forecasts are submitted at the Commercial Pricing (CP) node level by the Tariff Customer; MISO will monitor timeliness and accuracy against telemetered actual load and is considering incentive mechanisms (ranging from escalation to settlement-based penalties). Status: requirements finalized for LLWG feedback by July 13, 2026; accuracy incentives and BPM implementation to follow. For hydro operators, the mechanism is load-side variability management: large loads add volatile demand that MISO's standard weather/calendar forecasts cannot capture; if these forecasts are inaccurate, MISO's commitment stack and reserve procurement tighten or loosen unpredictably, affecting the scarcity signals and ramping/flexibility value hydro receives in real-time and look-ahead markets. The settlement-based penalty option (SPP precedent cited) could create a parallel market-discipline framework applied to demand-side forecast accuracy, potentially informing future treatment of hydro forecast errors and opportunity-cost offers.

title: 20260629 LLWG Item 09 Large Load Reserve Product Enhancements (LLWG 2026 2)

ai_summary: MISO has established a dynamic reserve requirement methodology that quantifies net uncertainty and derives seasonal reserve requirements for Regulation Reserve (4 sec–5 min timeframe), Ramp Capability Product (10 min), and Short-Term Reserve (30 min–3 hr), with requirements varying by season, region, and time of day. MISO will continue to monitor uncertainty patterns periodically and revise reserve methodologies if non-conforming load impact reaches criticality. Stakeholder feedback (six respondents, May 2026) was mostly supportive, and further engagement will occur at the Large Load Working Group.

title: 20260623 LOLEWG Item 03 Refresher on Seasonal LOLE Targets.pdf
relevance_reason: MISO's seasonal LOLE framework affects how hydro and other dispatchable resources are accredited in capacity adequacy studies and shapes seasonal RA requirements that determine hydro's reliability value and revenue exposure across quarters.
ai_summary: MISO adopted a seasonal LOLE (Loss of Load Expectation) construct in 2023–2024, replacing a single annual 0.1 days/year target with per-season minima of 0.01 days/year. The framework accounts for seasonal variation in peak load (winter mornings, overnight cold events), forced-outage rates (thermal units fail more in extreme cold/heat), planned maintenance clustering (spring/fall), and ELCC values for wind and solar, which differ materially by season. MISO runs an annual LOLE study first, then upwardly adjusts any season falling below 0.01 days/year by adding perfect or proxy units. This document presents the construct as positioned between PJM's simple annual PRMR% approach and ISO-NE's proposed monthly granularity, and includes historical LOLE splits (PY25–26 all summer risk; PY26–27 split summer/winter/spring; PY29–30 nearly even summer/winter) showing how seasonal requirements dampen year-to-year volatility. Hydro operators are most affected because seasonal accreditation directly determines their RA contribution value in each quarter—winter peaking and spring outage windows matter independently rather than being smoothed into a summer-anchored requirement—and because the tariff filing referenced as of June 1, 2026 (adding a perfect positive unit to the LOLE algorithm) may change the study's outcome.

ai_summary: MISO's Loss of Load Expectation Working Group is revising its load modeling process and load-forecast uncertainty assumptions for Planning Year 2027–2028, noting that actual loads have deviated from LOLE projections by 4% in shoulder seasons—exceeding current uncertainty bands. MISO is automating the load-development process (replacing NeuroShell with Histogram Gradient Boosting), standardizing extreme-temperature thresholds, and proposing to expand load-forecast error bands (e.g., from ±2% to a range including +3% to +4%) to reflect data-center and electrification-driven load growth. The key mechanism is that higher projected load peaks and wider uncertainty distributions increase the probability of scarcity conditions in LOLE runs, raising capacity-accreditation requirements for all dispatchable resources and making seasonal hydro availability more valuable in winter and shoulder months. MISO is requesting stakeholder feedback on model inputs and uncertainty-assumption options through July 7, 2026, via the Feedback Tool at misoenergy.org.

For hydro operators, tighter CIL/CEL values reduce their zone's ability to export capacity—lowering locational RA value and export revenue—while looser limits enhance those streams; the redispatch methodology's treatment of hydro as curtailable (not dispatchable) may understate the transfer capability available when hydro can flex output. Most exposed are multi-zone hydro fleets and pumped storage units in export-constrained Local Resource Zones.

title: 20260623 LOLEWG Item 07 Wind Profile Enhancement Update.pdf
relevance_reason: MISO's enhanced wind-profile methodology changes how wind and storage resources are accredited in ELCC and DLOL frameworks, directly affecting capacity-value revenue for dispatchable resources including pumped storage competing in MISO's resource-adequacy market.
ai_summary: MISO is adopting enhanced meteorology-driven wind profiles for its PY2027–2028 Loss of Load Expectation (LOLE) studies, replacing status-quo profiles with 30-year synthetic data that better capture low-wind conditions and seasonal variability. The new profiles increase wind ELCC values (especially in Spring, rising from 19.3% to 43.8%), but also shift the distribution of critical-event durations by season, causing storage DLOL accreditation to rise significantly in Fall (+12.7 percentage points) while falling in Winter and Spring (−11.2% and −20.0% respectively). Thermal resources' accreditation is affected primarily by shifts in which maintenance-outage hours overlap with newly identified critical hours. MISO plans to move forward with the enhanced profiles subject to final review and will maintain a hybrid approach (synthetic pre-2012, observed post-2012). This directly reshapes the seasonal accreditation profile for pumped-storage hydro competing in MISO's capacity market, particularly for four-hour-plus storage duration valuations.

title: 20260623 MISO-PJM JCM Item 02 Retirement of CTS Product.pdf
relevance_reason: MECHANISM: Retirement of CTS affects interregional energy scheduling and price convergence between MISO and PJM, which directly impacts dispatch economics and revenue for hydro resources located on or serving the MISO-PJM seam; loss of an interchange optimization tool reduces locational price signals and flexibility value for assets arbitraging between the RTOs.
ai_summary: MISO and PJM propose to retire the Coordinated Transaction Scheduling (CTS) product—a coordinated interchange optimization tool approved by FERC in 2016 and launched in 2017—due to minimal usage, underperformance ($740k in annual savings vs. $17–72M projected), and high migration costs ($1.4M to migrate to the new Market Clearing Engine, $0.8M to maintain over 5 years). Stakeholders submitted mixed feedback: some requested a modern replacement (e.g., SPP's Inter-Market Optimization) before retirement to avoid operational gaps, while others supported retirement given CTS inefficiencies. MISO responds that other interchange products (Fixed, Cleared Day-Ahead, and Dynamic schedules) already offer more granular, real-time scheduling (adjustable to 20 minutes before interval vs. 75 minutes for CTS), and MISO is open to pursuing replacement products with PJM and SPP after retirement. MISO and PJM intend to coordinate tariff and Joint Operating Agreement filings later in 2026 to remove CTS. Hydro owners on or serving the MISO-PJM interface lose a tool for optimizing interchange pricing and may see reduced locational value signals for flexibility; replacements under discussion are not yet defined.

title: 20260623 MISO-PJM JCM Item 03 MISO Interchange Ramp Rules Update.pdf
relevance_reason: MISO is removing interchange ramp restrictions for day-ahead offers, which directly affects how hydropower and other dispatchable resources can schedule power flows across MISO-PJM seams and influences flexibility/ramping product value.
ai_summary: MISO is eliminating restrictions on interchange ramp calculations for day-ahead market submissions, effective Q3 2026. Previously, MISO enforced limits of ±1000 MW on increased imports/decreased exports and +500 MW on increased exports/decreased imports, enforced via the Ramp Reservation System (RRS) for quarterly schedule changes. Removing these caps increases the scheduling flexibility available to hydro and other resources moving power across the MISO-PJM interface, allowing larger and more frequent interchange adjustments without pre-reservation denials. This particularly benefits reservoir-based hydropower and pumped storage that rely on schedule flexibility to optimize operations across interregional pricing signals; the change reduces a non-price scheduling constraint that previously limited their ability to respond to real-time conditions. Implementation is targeted for Q3 2026.

title: 20260623 MISO-PJM JCM Item 04 Interregional Planning Update.pdf

ai_summary: MISO and PJM are conducting a 2026 Coordinated System Plan (TMEP) to study interregional congestion on the MISO-PJM seam, targeting the remaining $681 million of persistent congestion after eliminating $441 million deemed non-persistent or addressable by planned upgrades. Twenty-three TMEP study candidates are under evaluation to identify limiting equipment and potential upgrades; the JRPC will make a recommendation to the Boards by November 2026. For hydro owners with generation located near the MISO-PJM seam or exporting capacity across it, transmission upgrades selected for mitigation will alter locational scarcity pricing and transfer capability — potentially increasing or decreasing the value of that hydro's energy sales into either region depending on which flowgates are relieved.

title: 20260617 AC Item 06 MISO Strategy Update

Hydro and pumped-storage operators must track revisions to regulation demand curves (4.8), performance adjustment rules (4.5–4.6), and resource qualification thresholds (4.11), as these directly affect the value of regulation and reserve services — historically hydro's largest ancillary-service revenue source in NYISO. The manual's treatment of energy storage resources in reactive power testing and performance frameworks may also signal NYISO's direction on storage parity rules relevant to pumped-storage PSH participation.

title: 5 Transmission Security Background
relevance_reason: NYISO's derating-factor methodology and transmission-security-assessment practices directly affect ICAP accreditation for all generators including hydropower, and the document addresses seasonal EFORd calculations and limited-control run-of-river hydro treatment in capacity-adequacy studies.
ai_summary: NYISO staff present transmission-security assessment background and derating-factor recommendations for the Installed Capacity market, including treatment of seasonal forced outage rates (EFORd) for thermal units and reference to run-of-river hydro derating under ICAP Manual Attachment N. The document identifies a methodological gap: 5-year seasonal EFORd averages understate zonal derating factors by roughly 2% compared to 5-year continuous EFORd, and NYISO recommends developing an automated tool to support multi-year continuous seasonal EFORd calculations. The implications for hydro are indirect but material—derating factors determine Locational Minimum Installed Capacity Requirements (LCRs) that shape the ICAP demand curve and pricing hydro and other resources bid into. Run-of-river resources are explicitly noted as following Attachment N methodology, though the document does not propose changes to that treatment in this June 2026 working-group meeting.

title: 6 Seasonal TSL Floor Kick Off
relevance_reason: NYISO's seasonal TSL floor methodology directly affects ICAP accreditation and capacity requirements for all resources including hydro and storage, with implications for winter peak conditions and derating factors for limited-control run-of-river hydro.
ai_summary: NYISO is implementing seasonal Transmission Security Limit (TSL) floor values as part of its Winter Reliability Capacity Enhancements proposal (filed with FERC February 18, 2026, Docket ER26-1431, effective date requested June 28, 2026, for 2027-2028 capability year onward). The seasonal methodology will replace annual calculations with winter- and summer-specific peak loads, bulk transmission limits, equipment ratings, and derating factors. Critically, NYISO proposes to include winter performance data for Limited Control Run of River hydro resources in the seasonal derating factor calculation and will establish winter-specific Special Case Resource (SCR) enrollment, which raises the ICAP addback component. The document indicates that 5-year derating factors will consider winter EFORd for thermal units and seasonal adjustments for intermittent and run-of-river hydro per updated ICAP Manual Attachment N (revised June 2026), and that seasonal External Unforced Deliverability Rights (UDR) elections would be implemented starting 2027-2028. Pumped storage and battery-based energy storage resources (ESRs) currently face no specific UCAP duration-limit adjustment in the TSL floor calculation, though the document notes ESRs are modeled in resource adequacy with full availability subject to duration limits. Run-of-river hydro owners should monitor the winter derating factor methodology to understand how winter-season performance data may reduce their seasonal ICAP accreditation; reservoir and pumped-storage operators should track the seasonal UDR election framework and any future ESR adjustments proposed.

title: 2 Winter Reliability Capacity Enhancements – Seasonal UDR/EDR Elections and Must Offer Requirement: Proposed ICAP Manual and Attachment Revisions
relevance_reason: NYISO establishes seasonal must-offer requirements and penalties for holders of External Unforced Capacity Deliverability Rights (UDRs) and External-to-Rest of State Deliverability Rights (EDRs), which directly affects how external capacity—including hydropower—can be exported from and must be offered to meet NYCA obligations, and creates an enforcement mechanism (penalty methodology in new Attachment Q) that changes an owner's compliance exposure and dispatch obligations.
ai_summary: NYISO is implementing seasonal elections for External UDRs and EDRs starting May 1, 2027 (2027–2028 Capability Year), with elections due August 1, 2026. Holders of External UDRs or EDRs must submit distinct seasonal elections (one for Summer, one for Winter) to return capacity to the NYCA, or face a must-offer requirement: capacity not returned must be offered in each ICAP Spot Market Auction or certified to meet LSE minimum UCAP requirements, and failure triggers a penalty calculated using Market Clearing Price and a new Attachment Q methodology converting ICAP to UCAP. This reshapes the options available to external capacity owners (including hydro exporters to NYCA) by forcing them to commit seasonally to either export or domestic service, with financial penalties for non-compliance; pumped-storage and reservoir hydro operators holding external rights into New York will need to evaluate seasonal dispatch strategies against the penalty risk. The proposal was filed with FERC in Docket No. ER26-1431 with requested effective date June 28, 2026; ICAP Manual revisions become effective one business day after the 10-day appeal period if approved (by July 7, 2026 absent appeal or FERC rejection).

title: 05a Summer 2026 Operations Study - Presentation

ai_summary: NYISO's Summer 2026 operations study reports 1,225 MW of generation retirements (including large thermal units like Danskammer 532 MW and Narrows 352 MW) offset by 225 MW of solar and storage additions. Major transmission projects—Champlain Hudson Power Express HVDC, Smart Path Connect 345 kV stations, and Hertel–Astoria additions—are now modeled in service. These changes redistribute flows and alter interface thermal limits: Total East interface limit decreased 125 MW, UPNY-ConEd increased 250 MW, UPNY-SENY increased 225 MW, and Moses South increased 250 MW. Sprain Brook Dunwoodie South interface limit was raised to 4,225 MW and Total East to 4,050 MW. The study's status is a June 2026 presentation update to the Operating Committee; no forward deadlines are stated. For hydro owners, the net effect is mixed: retirement of thermal generation reduces dispatchable competition and may elevate real-time energy prices and ramping value, while the HVDC and transmission upgrades improve northern import capability and may compress NY price separations, affecting both in-state dispatchable hydro revenue and Northwest-to-NY export economics. Pumped-storage operators should monitor how the reduced Moses South thermal limits and increased UPNY interfaces change the voltage-support and frequency-response service opportunities in those zones.

For hydro interconnection customers, a 'fully deliverable' determination removes the risk of being forced to undersize their injection or fund costly network upgrades to achieve their requested MW — streamlining path to commercial operation. title: 4a MST 26.4 redline

ai_summary: NYISO's Market Monitoring Unit (Potomac Economics) identifies structural gaps in the capacity market that undervalue reliability contributions and distort investment incentives. Key findings: (1) demand curves based on 2-hour battery cost understate Net CONE, risking premature retirements even as load grows; (2) seasonal incentives are misaligned—firm fuel/UDR elections locked 16 months in advance don't respond to winter market prices, and elected capacity for 2026/27 (15.2 GW) exceeds planning assumptions (12.3 GW), creating cost-allocation risk; (3) transmission security is undercompensated—downstate LCRs increasingly bind at floor, overpaying bottled generation (SCRs, large units) and underpaying non-firm gas units while creating $74M annual inefficiency post-CHPE. Recommendations filed or pending include raising the demand-curve floor (Rec. 2025-1a), moving seasonal-election deadlines closer to winter (Rec. 2022-2), introducing locational CAFs (Rec. 2025-2), and expanding capacity zones. These touch pumped-storage accreditation (2-hour battery CONE undermines longer-duration PSH value), seasonal energy adequacy (firm fuel elections timing), and locational value recognition (hydro deliverability and transmission-security contribution). No formal comment deadline is stated in this highlights presentation, but the full 2025 SOM Report (posted May 19, 2026) and tariff filing ER26-1431 are the operative documents.

title: 3 Automatic ICAP Surplus Offers
relevance_reason: MECHANISM: NYISO is revising the ICAP market's surplus-offer rules to automatically resell capacity that load-serving entities and ICAP suppliers procure but do not need, at zero-dollar bids. For hydropower and storage owners selling capacity into NYISO's ICAP market—whether as primary capacity suppliers or via bilateral trades—this rule removes their option to withhold surplus capacity and directly affects the monetization path and price realization for unsold UCAP.
ai_summary: NYISO proposes a new tariff section (5.14.4) that automatically submits zero-dollar offers for any Unforced Capacity (UCAP) surplus held by load-serving entities, ICAP suppliers, and ICAP marketers after the monthly certification deadline, effective May 1, 2027 (Board approval and FERC filing required). Currently, surplus UCAP often goes unoffered, potentially raising market-clearing prices; the automatic zero-dollar offer guarantees resale at the auction clearing price. Hydropower and pumped-storage owners—particularly those acquiring capacity via bilateral trades or selling excess UCAP—will face mandatory resale of any certified surplus, eliminating the ability to withhold capacity or negotiate off-market prices for unexpectedly available MW; however, capacity associated with a physical transmission interface (PTID) and 'unoffered MW' remain subject to physical-withholding rules and are excluded from automatic resale.

ai_summary: Brattle Group presents PJM staff analysis of market-power mitigation (MPM) rules applied to battery energy storage, arguing that conventional fuel-based mitigation caps—designed for fossil generators—are poorly fitted to storage resources and cause two problems: (1) capping mitigated offers below inter-hour opportunity cost causes early, inefficient discharge and misallocates stored energy away from peak-scarcity hours, reducing reliability; (2) PJM's t-65-minute offer-price lock prevents sellers from updating offers as conditions change, locking in discharge decisions that become counterproductive when actual prices spike (illustrated by Winter Storm Elliott case study showing 42% of battery SOC misallocated). ai_summary: PJM's Board has approved a two-path Reliability Backstop Procurement (RBP) mechanism to address a megawatt shortfall in the 2028/2029 Base Residual Auction, combining a central procurement administered by PJM and a facilitated bilateral matchmaking process. The RBP will procure long-term capacity-only UCAP commitments for a fixed 15-year term from 2028/2029 DY to 2042/2043 DY, structured as pay-as-bid offers in $/MW-day with a maximum willingness-to-pay cap of $555/MW-day UCAP (Point 1 of the unconstrained 2028/2029 BRA VRR Curve). Resources with RBP commitments become PJM capacity resources subject to a mandatory RPM Must-Offer Obligation at $0 (price taker) and are settled as contracts for differences against weighted-average RPM clearing prices. The central procurement window runs September 30 to October 21, 2026, with selection and results October 22 to December 2, 2026. Resources face a 20% shortfall-charge rate (based on RBP commitment price) if delayed or failing to come online, with a 3-year delay threshold triggering commitment rescission. Cost allocation is pro rata by zone/area based on load-growth megawatts, and resources must post collateral equal to 0.2 × (RBP Sell Offer Price × committed UCAP × 365 × 3 years). The framework includes provisions for Transmission Owner exit scenarios and default allocation among LSEs.

ai_summary: GridLab presents a diagnosis of PJM's capacity market (RPM) and proposes eliminating it in favor of energy-market-only design with scarcity pricing and bilateral contracts. On interconnection, the presentation argues that PJM's emphasis on deliverability and network-upgrade modeling has created a 'vicious cycle' of queue delays and project dropout, and advocates point-of-interconnection upgrades and study-speed reduction as practiced by ERCOT; modeling analysis cited from Telos claims curtailment does not occur during resource-adequacy events in PJM, suggesting transmission constraints are not a limiting factor for resource contribution. On transmission planning, the presentation references SPP's Consolidated Planning Process as a model for proactive multi-value expansion. The document does not propose specific regulatory changes or announce a next step within PJM's governance.
hydro_read_through: This document does not mention hydropower or pumped storage. However, the core argument — replacing PJM's capacity market with scarcity pricing and bilateral contracts — would reshape how all dispatchable resources, including hydro and storage, are accredited and rewarded. A capacity-market elimination would remove the seasonal ELCC accreditation process and shift revenue entirely to energy-market scarcity events and contract negotiation, fundamentally altering the revenue stability and seasonal pricing hydro owners rely on. Additionally, the interconnection critique attacks the current deliverability-based queue management; if PJM adopted ERCOT-style point-of-interconnection-only upgrades, it would reduce pre-operational network costs for new generation, lowering barriers to entry for competing resources (especially fast-ramping ones) and intensifying competitive pressure on hydro's energy and flexibility margins.

ai_summary: PJM Manual M14D Revision 71 clarifies voltage and reactive-power control requirements for generators 20 MVA and above, establishing that only automatic voltage control mode (AVR controlling voltage) is acceptable without documented exception. The revision defines volt-var boundaries at ±32.87% of maximum MW output, specifies acceptable reactive-control range per MW output, and requires PJM approval for any deviation from automatic voltage mode. A three-party investigation process is established for reactive-control performance issues. The changes respond to NERC's May 15, 2026 lowering of IBR registration thresholds to 20 MVA (bringing mid-sized inverter-based resources under Category 2 GO registration) and PJM's stated concern about increasing low-voltage risks, exemplified by the 2025 Spain blackout in which insufficient synchronous-generator voltage support contributed to a major outage.

However, conventional synchronous hydropower plants—especially large run-of-river and reservoir facilities—are among PJM's primary sources of dynamic voltage support and will be directly subject to these tightened automatic-voltage-control requirements and the new D-curve boundaries. Hydro owners operating in PJM must now ensure their AVR equipment is configured to automatic voltage mode unless they obtain explicit documented exemptions from both PJM and the transmission owner; plants already running in constant-MVAR or constant-power-factor mode will require engineering review and possible operational changes. The higher clarity on volt-var boundaries may also change how hydro operators bid reactive-power capability into PJM's voltage-schedule process, affecting both revenue opportunities and compliance risk if their equipment cannot meet the new boundaries.
