ai_summary: PJM has implemented a new Expedited Interconnection Track (EIT) process as a parallel track to the standard interconnection queue for generators meeting three criteria: (1) written support from a Primary Siting Authority, (2) commercial operation within 36 months, and (3) at least 250 MW of Accredited UCAP. The EIT process compresses interconnection review into three phases—Application Review (~180 days), Study (~60 days), and Final Agreement Negotiation (~60 days)—operating outside but parallel to the PJM Cycle Adequacy Process to expedite state-sponsored generation projects. PJM filed EIT tariff revisions with FERC on April 9, 2026 (Docket No. ER26-1563) and submitted a Limited Effective Date Answer and Amendment on July 31, 2026. Manual 14H revisions to implement the EIT process were endorsed by the Planning Committee on June 24, 2026, and received first reading at the Markets and Reliability Committee on July 7, 2026, with final endorsement scheduled for July 28, 2026.
hydro_read_through: The document does not mention hydropower or pumped storage. However, the 250 MW UCAP threshold and tight 36-month development timeline make the EIT track potentially accessible to larger run-of-river or peaking hydro plants and pumped-storage projects with state backing seeking to qualify for resource-adequacy accreditation faster than standard-queue timelines allow. The elimination of milestone-extension options (blocking the one-time postponement available in standard GIA processes) imposes stricter compliance discipline on expedited applicants, which would tighten capital and permitting schedules for hydro developers pursuing this path versus the standard process.

ai_summary: PJM Manual 14H (New Service Requests Cycle Process), Revision 06, incorporates conforming changes for the new Expedited Interconnection Track (EIT) process per FERC Docket No. ER26-1563-000. The revision adds Section 16 (EIT Overview and Process in sections 16.1–16.5) and Attachment L, and updates multiple sections including the application and final-agreement provisions. The manual governs interconnection procedures for generation, transmission, merchant transmission, and Long Term Firm Transmission Service requests submitted to PJM, including phases and decision points, cost allocation for Network Upgrades and Interconnection Facilities, site control requirements, and deposit schedules. The revision is effective July 23, 2026, and approved December 8, 2025.
hydro_read_through: The document does not mention hydropower or storage directly. Faster interconnection timelines and any changes to how deliverability rights, cost responsibility, and Network Upgrades are studied and allocated under the EIT process will establish baselines that apply to hydro developers in parallel with thermal and renewable projects. Hydro owners should monitor which project types are eligible for EIT and whether the accelerated study cycles affect the cost and timing of their own interconnection requests.

ai_summary: PJM GDECS (Governing Document Enhancements Cleanup Series) April 2026 package proposes seventeen tariff revisions to Attachment DD (Reliability Pricing Model), Operating Agreement, and interconnection procedures. Key changes: (1) Capacity Storage Resources and Intermittent Resources must now offer as annual (not seasonal) into RPM Auctions, with the categorical must-offer exception removed per FERC 190 FERC ¶ 61,117 (2025); (2) Commercial aggregation of these resources limited to those granted additional winter Capacity Interconnection Rights; (3) UCAP definition revised to align with effective load-carrying capability (ELCC) analysis per Schedule 9.2; (4) Planned Generation Capacity Resources that clear an RPM Auction become Existing Generation Capacity Resources for subsequent Incremental Auctions in the same Delivery Year; (5) Mixed-Technology Facility definitions clarified for participation as single ELCC Resource or multiple stand-alone resources, with five-year modeling election periods. DER Capacity Aggregation Resources subject to MOPR Floor Offer Price and Market Seller Offer Cap per March 1, 2023 FERC Order (paragraph 87). Document appears on PJM MRC consent agenda for 2026-07-28 meeting; no comment deadline stated in excerpt.
hydro_read_through: The document does not mention hydropower or pumped-storage facilities by name, but the revisions directly govern resource types to which hydro and PSH are subject or compete with. Removal of the must-offer categorical exception for Capacity Storage Resources and Intermittent Resources means PSH and conventional hydro's seasonal flexibility value faces heightened must-offer obligations for annual capacity commitments—affecting their auction bidding strategies and accreditation calculations. The ELCC-aligned UCAP definition will rebase how hydro's seasonal and peak-period capacity is accredited: owners will need to track effective load-carrying capability analysis rather than EFORd-based forced-outage rates, directly changing seasonal accreditation factors and thus capacity-market revenue. The aggregation limits and five-year modeling elections for mixed-technology facilities also matter if hydro co-locations with solar or battery storage are pursued. MOPR and Market Seller Offer Cap rules applying to DER aggregations set a pathway and precedent affecting how small hydro may participate in future Order 2222 aggregation pilots.

ai_summary: PJM proposes to refine the definition of 'flexible resources' to require that resources meet flexibility criteria (combined startup and notification time of 2 hours or less, minimum run time of 2 hours or less) on all available offer schedules, not just some. Under the proposal, resources that do not meet this criterion on all available schedules would be treated as inflexible for real-time operation and lost-opportunity-cost (LOC) purposes. The tightening of the definition to require flexibility across all available schedules could reduce the ability of units with operational constraints (e.g., those that are flexible only on certain cost-based schedules) to claim LOC credits when curtailed, affecting the risk-reward calculus for committing inflexible capacity day-ahead.

ai_summary: The Deactivation Enhancement (DESTF) Phase II Scope Status Report presents PJM's framework for managing generator deactivations. Phase II scope addresses three new areas: (1) procedures to evaluate grid-enhancing technologies, reconductoring, demand-side management, and energy storage as long-term transmission solutions to avoid Reliability Must-Run (RMR) contracts; (2) alternative solutions to RMR contracts including new generation assets, energy storage, demand-side solutions, transmission enhancements, generation-replacement proposals from deactivating generators (CIR transfers), and accelerated interconnection processing, with evaluation frameworks comparing costs and benefits across resource types; and (3) a pro forma RMR arrangement and capacity market rule updates for deactivating generators temporarily retained for reliability. Three proposals were developed for Scope Areas 4/5 (PJM, Coalition, and Independent Market Monitor), none achieving >50% support; for Scope Area 6 (pro forma RMR), PJM's proposal received >50% support and preference over status quo, and is offered for consideration at the June 24, 2026 Markets & Reliability Committee meeting.
hydro_read_through: The document does not mention hydropower or pumped storage directly. However, Phase II addresses how PJM will treat deactivating generators facing reliability retention through RMR contracts and what alternatives to RMR exist—a critical issue for aging or economically stressed hydro plants. The framework's treatment of "new generation assets" and "energy storage" as alternatives to RMR, and PJM's obligation to evaluate competing solutions and their costs, will set precedent for whether retiring hydro can be replaced by storage, demand-side resources, or transmission upgrades, and what retention compensation would look like if a hydro asset is deemed necessary for reliability. The Scope Area 6 proposal advancing to committee vote will determine the pro forma terms hydro owners face if they seek to operate under RMR rather than deactivate.

ai_summary: PJM's redlined tariff amendment to Attachment DD, Section 5.3, modifies the treatment of Generation Capacity Resources committed through Reliability Must Run Service Agreements or transmission-retention rate schedules. Resources that do not clear the Base Residual Auction but meet specified criteria—including obligation to operate throughout the Delivery Year and FERC acceptance of the rate schedule at least three months prior to planning-parameter posting—are deemed to submit a Sell Offer at $0/MW-Day for their full Accredited UCAP (up to Capacity Interconnection Rights) in the Base Residual Auction. ai_summary: PJM is revising Manual 14H to adopt IEEE 2800-2022 interconnection requirements for inverter-based resources (IBRs) in Phase 1, covering definitions, ride-through specifications, and primary frequency response parameters. The revision creates new Section 9.15 and Attachment K, effective June 22, 2027, and applies to IBRs interconnecting with transmission and sub-transmission systems. Key technical parameters include enter-service voltage thresholds (0.9–1.05 p.u.), frequency ranges (58.8–60.12 Hz), and voltage ride-through times ranging from 0.16 to 1800 seconds depending on voltage magnitude; frequency disturbance ride-through requirements exclude fast frequency response. PJM Markets and Reliability Committee is scheduled for first read July 28, 2026, with Planning Committee first read May 8, 2026 and endorsement votes on June 2 and August 19, 2026.
hydro_read_through: The document does not mention conventional hydropower or pumped-storage resources. However, the ride-through and frequency-response standards being adopted apply to the general category of synchronous and grid-forming resources interconnecting at the transmission level, which includes conventional hydro units. Hydro owners in PJM would need to assess whether existing units meet the mandated voltage and frequency ride-through envelope (particularly the 0.16–0.32 second ride-through times at very low voltages) and the primary frequency response droops and deadbands; units falling short could face retrofit costs or operational restrictions. The June 22, 2027 effective date would establish new technical requirements for any plant modifications or uprates proposed by that deadline.

ai_summary: PJM Manual 21B Revision 06 (effective June 24, 2026) specifies the rules and procedures for determining generating capability and ELCC accreditation across all resource classes in the PJM capacity market. The manual defines two hydro-specific ELCC classes: Intermittent Hydropower Class (run-of-river resources that cannot appreciably store water) and Hydropower With Non-Pumped Storage (resources that can capture and store incoming streamflow and exert material control over output—demonstrated by producing at least 110% of daily average power baseline for 4 hours during the four highest load hours of summer afternoons over a five-year rolling period). Existing Hydropower With Non-Pumped Storage resources failing this evaluation may be reclassified as Intermittent Hydropower, though PJM may retain the prior classification for exceptional circumstances including "recreational and public safety factors, unit outages, locational market energy prices, ancillary market participation, and other exceptional operational factors or market factors." Testing requirements differ by class: Hydro with Non-Pumped Storage units must conduct one-hour contiguous capability verification tests (summer June 1–September 1, deadline September 20; winter December 1–March 1, deadline March 20), while Limited Duration Resources' test duration must equal their applicable ELCC Class characteristic duration. The manual also defines Hybrid Resource Classes (including combinations of storage with variable or unlimited resources) and Component DER frameworks for distributed energy resources, all subject to ELCC-based accreditation.
hydro_read_through: Hydro owners' capacity-market accreditation and seasonal revenue now turn critically on ELCC class assignment. The material-control test for conventional (non-pumped) storage hydro—requiring 110% of daily average output for 4 hours in the four highest summer load hours over five rolling years—creates a measurable but stringent threshold; failure triggers reclassification to intermittent status and a steep loss of accredited MW. PJM's discretion to retain prior classification for "exceptional circumstances" including ancillary-market participation and market-driven operational constraints opens a compliance and advocacy pathway, but the burden is on the owner to document and request relief. Testing deadlines (September 20 summer, March 20 winter) and single-hour duration for conventional hydro are tighter than multi-hour Limited Duration Resources, reflecting the traditional assumption that hydro can ramp quickly; owners must plan annual test coordination with PJM Dispatch. Hybrid resource rules now formally accommodate co-located storage and variable resources at a single point of interconnection, expanding options for hydro owners seeking to blend storage or renewable capacity into a single market-accredited asset—a significant strategic opening if ELCC accreditation for hybrids is favorable.

ai_summary: PJM is implementing Regulation Redesign Phase 2 on December 1, 2026, replacing its one-signal bidirectional regulation product with two separate products: RegUp (operates above zero crossing) and RegDn (operates below zero crossing). Regulation market participants (including hydro operators) must submit RegUp/RegDn offers and parameters to the Markets Gateway sandbox immediately (deadline overdue), complete signal conversion testing (overdue), and prepare for cutover by December 1, 2026; a virtual open house is scheduled July 30, 2026, and special education sessions occur October–November 2026. ai_summary: PJM is conducting a periodic cover-to-cover review of Manual 21B, which establishes the accreditation framework for capacity resources. Changes include clarification of the ICAP definition, updated testing rules around ambient conditions and simultaneous requirements, codification of test-data requirements in a new Appendix A, explicit permission to gather additional data for ELCC analysis, and updates to the Performance Adjustment section for distributed-energy-resource calculations. The document is in first read before the Planning Committee (July 7, 2026); second read and endorsement are scheduled for August 4, with MRC consideration on August 19. These changes affect how hydro and especially pumped-storage capacity accreditation is measured, tested, and adjusted — a direct lever on PSH and reservoir-hydro RA value in PJM's market. The timing suggests comments or questions from stakeholders would be most useful before the August endorsement.

The changes will go to MRC first read on July 28, 2026 and voting on August 19, 2026. For hydro and pumped-storage operators, the clarified ELCC data-collection pathway and updated performance-adjustment methodology may alter how their capacity contributions are measured and credited in PJM's accreditation process.

title: Item 05 – 1 Manual 14h Revisions Ids – Presentation
relevance_reason: Interconnection and deliverability rules for new resources directly affect when hydro and storage projects can enter service and begin generating revenue; the cluster-based methodology change alters how PJM allocates deliverable capacity among competing projects, which shapes project developer economics and must-offer obligations.
ai_summary: PJM proposes revising Manual 14-H to transition the Interim Deliverability Study (IDS) from serial to cluster-based methodology, effective 2027/2028 Delivery Year. The proposal introduces two subclusters: Subcluster 1 prioritizes projects already provisionally operational from prior IDS results, while Subcluster 2 includes all new IDS requests; deliverable MW are allocated proportionally within each subcluster using distribution factors (DFAX). PJM argues this mitigates developer risk of curtailment for projects deemed deliverable in prior years but enhances operational certainty and Capacity Market alignment; the current alternative is a single-cluster approach where all projects compete equally, creating higher curtailment risk for provisionally operational resources. Planning Committee first read is July 7, 2026; voting is scheduled August 4, 2026, with MRC vote August 19 and an October 30 effective date for 2027/28 IDS results—timing is compressed because the 2027/28 application window closed June 30, 2026 and results must be completed by October 2026. Developers whose projects are already provisionally operational will benefit most from the two-subcluster design, as it preserves their must-offer status and operational continuity; new applicants face greater delivery uncertainty.

title: Item 05 – 2 Manual 14h Revisions Ids – Problem Statement
relevance_reason: Interim Deliverability Study methodology changes affect hydropower and storage project deliverability accreditation and capacity-market participation in PJM, touching both resource-adequacy positioning and interconnection strategic options for existing and new hydro assets.
ai_summary: PJM proposes enhancements to its Interim Deliverability Study (IDS) methodology under Manual 14H to stabilize deliverability determinations across delivery years and reduce risk that generating resources with Provisional Interconnection Service lose deliverability status in subsequent years. The problem statement identifies that the current sequential, project-by-project IDS approach creates year-over-year volatility in deliverability outcomes and misalignment between planning study results and real-time operational/capacity-market obligations, particularly under PJM's transition to Cycle-based interconnection. The enhancement aims to provide greater predictability, align study outcomes with must-offer obligations into future delivery years, and recognize operational realities of resources already generating—mechanisms that directly affect how existing hydro and pumped-storage resources maintain deliverability accreditation and capacity-market eligibility. This is in problem-statement phase; no comment deadline or vote date is stated in this excerpt.

title: Item 05 – 3 Manual 14h Revisions Ids – Issue Charge

title: Item 05 – 5 Manual 14h Revisions Ids – Redline
relevance_reason: INTERCONNECTION: Manual 14H revisions redefine interim deliverability study procedures and cluster-based allocation methodology for new resources seeking Provisional Interconnection Service, directly affecting project-queue timing, capacity-rights assignment, and transmission-constrained resource entry for hydro and storage projects.
ai_summary: PJM Manual 14H revisions establish a new cluster-based methodology for interim deliverability studies, effective with the 2027/2028 Delivery Year. Subcluster 1 prioritizes previously provisionally operational projects, while Subcluster 2 includes all other eligible projects; deliverable megawatts are allocated proportionally within each cluster using DFAX methodology. Projects must request interim studies at least 11 months before the target Delivery Year and may be granted Provisional Interconnection Service (at PJM's discretion, as energy-only for projects with Contingent Facilities), valid only for that specific Delivery Year. The cluster methodology materially changes the queue-management signal: projects already operating under prior provisional status receive priority in allocation, while new entrants (including hydro projects seeking early entry) compete in a secondary tier, making repeated interim-study cycles necessary for multi-year deferrals. This affects timing and certainty of capacity interconnection rights for any hydro or pumped-storage project planning to enter PJM before baseline RTEP study completion.

ai_summary: PJM/Dominion presented supplemental transmission projects to the Transmission Expansion Advisory Committee on July 7, 2026, addressing operational bottlenecks and load growth in Dominion's Virginia transmission zone. Key drivers include: (1) chronic low-voltage conditions and reactive-power scarcity in the Prince William County load pocket during outages—currently mitigated by a temporary mobile capacitor bank—exacerbated by continued data-center load growth (DOM-2026-0026); (2) multiple do-no-harm violations triggered by new customer interconnections requiring transformer upgrades and line rebuilds in the Meadowville, James Hill, Tropical, and Orrock load areas (projects budgeted $17.5M–$212M, mostly in-service Q4 2031); and (3) two smaller distribution upgrades in Herndon and Prince William County serving non-data-center load by end-2027/2028. The Meadowville project (DOM-2019-0021, DOM-2024-0022/23/24) represents the most significant constraint, with a 300+ MW N-1-1 contingency violation by 2029 requiring new substations and dual 230 kV lines. Hydro owners should monitor whether these transmission investments will increase the scarcity value of voltage support and reactive-power reserves that reservoir hydro can supply during shoulder months and peak periods in a load-constrained region; conversely, transmission relief may reduce ancillary-service revenue in the zone.

title: PJM Board Whitepaper
relevance_reason: Transmission expansion planning directly affects hydro deliverability, interregional transfer capability, and the viability of large-load interconnections (including data-center co-location) that shape the scarcity value of existing hydro generation.
ai_summary: PJM's TEAC recommended and the Board approved (July 14, 2026) a net $1.17 billion decrease to the Regional Transmission Expansion Plan (RTEP), reflecting cancellations of New Jersey offshore-wind-driven projects ($1.04B reduction), scope/cost changes to existing baseline projects (net $119M reduction), and new baseline reliability projects ($22M addition). These transmission modifications reshape interregional transfer paths and local congestion patterns; the data-center co-location upgrade in particular signals load-driven scarcity in mid-Atlantic zones that could raise energy and reserve prices where hydro can deliver. No comment deadline or next procedural step is stated in this staff whitepaper.

title: Item 06 – EDART Auto Ticket Creation – Presentation
relevance_reason: Affects how hydro and PSH owners must report generator availability and forced outages to PJM, touching both dispatch obligations and the accuracy of outage data that feeds forced-outage rates used in capacity accreditation and forecasting.
ai_summary: PJM is implementing automatic eDART (Outage Database) ticket creation in September 2026 to capture all unavailable MW from committed capacity resources in real time. The system will auto-generate forced-outage tickets when a unit shows unavailable in Markets Gateway but lacks an active outage ticket in eDART, closing a gap exposed by Winter Storm Elliott and reinforced by Winter Storm Fern where unplanned outages went unreported. This directly affects hydro and PSH operators' obligation to report unavailable capacity timely and accurately under Schedule 1 Section 1.10.1A(d) (must-offer rules); the auto-creation logic will flag operators whose availability data in Markets Gateway diverges from eDART submissions, and forced-outage rates derived from eDART feed into capacity accreditation, reserve calculations, and PJM's forecast accuracy to stakeholders. Hydro and PSH owners dependent on accurate outage reporting for capacity value and performance assessment should monitor the Tech Change and eDART forums as details are formalized before the September 2026 implementation.

title: Item 04 – Market Participation Options For Mixed Technology Facilities
relevance_reason: Defines participation pathways (co-located vs. hybrid models) and capacity/must-offer rules affecting how mixed-technology resources—including pumped-storage hydro paired with other resources—can be classified, accredited, and dispatched in PJM markets, with direct implications for hybrid PSH revenue and operational flexibility.
stakeholders: Amanda Martin (PJM); Dave Miscavage (PJM); Maria Belenky (PJM)
ai_summary: PJM's Interconnection Process Subcommittee presented market participation options for Mixed Technology Facilities (MTF)—facilities with multiple generation or storage types behind a single interconnection point. Resources can participate as independent Co-Located Resources (each a separate market unit) or as a Hybrid Resource (single market unit with unit-specific accreditation). A closed-loop hybrid with storage can charge from grid; an open-loop hybrid cannot. Facilities with independent components can elect either model; those with significant interdependency (e.g., storage unable to charge from grid) must use the hybrid model. Classification must be declared 6 months before in-service date; capacity resources must choose the same model for both capacity and energy markets and must re-elect within RAA Schedule 9.2 deadlines; energy-only resources can change election once per calendar year with notice by May 30. For any MTF, the site Maximum Facility Output (MFO) cannot be exceeded in real time and capacity-must-offer obligations apply to the original Certified Interconnection Rights. The four use cases illustrate that inverter-gen + storage (like solar + battery or wind + battery) and non-inverter gen + storage (gas + battery) can form hybrids, while non-inverter gen + inverter gen (gas + solar) must participate as co-located resources. This framework directly affects pumped-storage hydro owners considering co-location with other generation or considering participation in paired-resource models, constraining how PSH state-of-charge management interacts with capacity accreditation and must-offer rules.

Timeline: Replacement Generation went live April 2026; Expedited Interconnection Track is July 2026; Surplus goes live August/September 2026; Upgrade track rollout TBD. title: Item 02 – Pjms Rcstf Proposal Summary

initiatives: Reserve Certainty and Resource Flexibility Incentives [solution alternatives proposed]
ai_summary: PJM proposes restructuring its reserve construct to align scheduling with operational needs and address growing ramping and uncertainty requirements. The proposal introduces three new reserve products—10-minute Ramp and Uncertainty (RUR), 10-minute Ramp and Uncertainty Down, and 30-minute RUR—each with specified offer caps ($10/MWh day-ahead, $0 real-time), balancing settlement, and locational procurement. These products carry fast response requirements (10–30 min) that hydro and PSH are positioned to supply, and are priced at 1.25× the clearing price or cost-to-provide, whichever is higher. The proposal also shifts Day-Ahead Scheduling Reserve from a fixed 4.51%-of-peak formula to a dynamic, risk-based framework classified by operating-day conditions. Hydro and pumped-storage operators will directly participate in procurement of these ramping/flexibility products, which represent new revenue streams for fast-responding resources; exposure depends on portfolio flexibility and locational advantage. The document does not state a vote date or comment deadline.

title: Item 03a – Imm Rcstf Presentation
relevance_reason: PJM's reserve product redesign proposal directly affects hydro revenue through reserve-clearing incentives, online/offline reserve mix, and reserve performance accountability — reserve-eligible hydro and PSH earn revenue from reserve provision and market-efficiency changes that alter clearing prices and call-out frequency.
initiatives: Reserve Certainty and Resource Flexibility Incentives [solution alternatives proposed]
ai_summary: The Independent Market Monitor (IMM) presents its interim reserve-redesign proposal for PJM's Reliability Committee, opposing PJM's parallel proposal. The IMM recommends three sequential implementation packages: (1) incorporating net load forecast uncertainty into reserve calculations (near-term priority); (2) reserve performance measurement and settlement changes; (3) reserve eligibility and market-clearing engine changes. The critical difference is the online/offline reserve mix: PJM proposes all 10-minute reserves be online-only, significantly raising production costs and clearing prices; the IMM proposes maintaining offline reserve capability (primary reserves) and synchronized (online) reserves separately. The IMM contends PJM's approach reduces market efficiency and jeopardizes reliability if current fast-start generators drop fast-start capability to avoid the online-reserve requirement. Solar generation in PJM has grown dramatically (14.3 GW maximum hourly output in 2026, 2.4% of annual generation), driving net-load uncertainty that both proposals address but with different reserve adequacy methods — the IMM's approach captures generator performance uncertainty in 30-minute reserves and includes demand response as eligible supply. No vote date or next-step deadline is stated; the presentation positions the IMM proposal as the operational-necessity baseline against PJM's preferred-design alternative.

ai_summary: PJM's Advanced Analytics team analyzed 2025 real-time market pricing impacts from proposed multi-step Operating Reserve Demand Curves (ORDCs) unnesting 10-minute Synchronized Reserve from 30-minute reserves and creating explicit 30-minute and 10-minute Online Reserve products. The Full Case scenario (updated ORDCs with Primary Reserve not clearing) showed 10-minute Online reserve prices rising from $10.25/MWh to $13.04/MWh (+$2.79), energy LMPs rising $0.80/MWh, uplift declining 3.8%, and load reserve payments rising $216M for 10-minute Online reserves—with greatest price pressure during peak hours when reserves are most needed. The simulation found that prepositioning units with ramping products in the multi-step ORDC case reduced scarcity-event frequency compared to the base case, particularly during two modeled shortage events (3/3/2025 and 8/12/2025), suggesting improved reserve-positioning efficiency, though the analysis carries limitations (PROBE PD simulation tool, combustion-turbine-only commitment, 30-minute Online requirement added to SR requirement rather than separately modeled). Document presented to RCSTF with no stated vote or deadline; further results posted post-presentation.

title: Consent Agenda B – 1 Manual 11 Revisions Advance Scheduled Resources Phase 1 – Presentation

initiatives: Resource Scheduling Prior to the Day Ahead Energy Market [evaluation in progress]
ai_summary: PJM has formalized Manual 11 revisions implementing advance pre-scheduling of generation resources with start-up or notification times exceeding 24 hours, committing them to cost-based offers prior to the day-ahead market close to ensure resource availability during forecasted system emergencies (lessons from Winter Storm Elliott). Resources pre-scheduled in advance must be committed on cost-based schedules subject to Fuel Cost Policy rules; those with >24-hour start times cannot update cost-based offers after advance scheduling, while shorter start-time resources may update cost-based offers only through the day-ahead market. The revision locks the 'Switch to Cost Schedule' flag automatically for advance-scheduled units, preventing market sellers from reverting to price-based schedules for the scheduled operating days. Most exposed are slow-start hydroelectric and pumped-storage units (>24-hour commitment lead time) in PJM's footprint, which lose offer flexibility during emergency conditions but gain certainty of commitment; the practical revenue effect depends on whether cost-based offer caps reflect true opportunity cost. title: Item 01 – 1 Schedule 2 Penalties – Presentation

initiatives: Schedule 2 Penalty Calculations [awaiting implementation & ferc approval]
ai_summary: PJM proposes revising Operating Agreement Schedule 2 section 6.1 penalty formulae to prevent Market Sellers from receiving credits (negative penalties) when cost-based offers are non-compliant and real-time LMPs are negative. The revised formula introduces an error-identification factor (E = 0.25 for self-reported errors, 1 otherwise), a market-impact factor (I) that escalates penalties if non-compliance continues after PJM or MMU notice, and a duration multiplier (d) capping at 15 days. This change tightens enforcement of offer compliance for all dispatchable and storage resources subject to cost-based offer rules—hydro and PSH are typically among resources required to submit cost-based offers, so stricter penalties and elimination of negative-penalty loopholes increases the cost of offer errors and reinforces compliance discipline. First Read was May 20, 2026; Markets & Reliability Committee vote scheduled June 24, 2026.

initiatives: Schedule 2 Penalty Calculations [awaiting implementation & ferc approval]
ai_summary: PJM's Markets and Reliability Committee is revising Schedule 2 penalties for non-compliant cost-based offers. The redline text establishes a two-tier penalty structure: (1) a non-escalating penalty using a formula weighted by LMP, available capacity, a self-identification factor (0.25 if self-reported, 1.0 otherwise), and a market-impact factor that ranges from 0.1 to 1.0 depending on whether the resource cleared, ran, passed pivotal-supplier tests, or submitted offers above $1,000/MWh; and (2) a daily escalating penalty (multiplied by day count d, starting at 2 and capping at 15) for continuing violations after PJM notification. Hydro operators subject to cost-based offer requirements—particularly pumped storage and run-of-river resources with use-limited characteristics—face heightened compliance costs if offer errors persist; the escalating penalty's cap at day 15 and the incentive structure (lower penalties for self-reported errors) will shape whether operators err on the side of conservative offers or market-responsive pricing. No comment deadline or vote date is stated in this redline.

title: Item 02 – 1 Manual 13 Annual Review Revisions – Presentation

stakeholders: Lisa Drauschak (PJM); Mike Handlin (PJM); Paul Dajewski (PJM)
ai_summary: PJM approved Manual 13 Revision 98 (effective July 23, 2026) updating emergency operations procedures to align with NERC EOP-011 standards and address capacity-deficient conditions occurring outside traditional weather-alert triggers. Key changes include: (1) a new Capacity Advisory mechanism providing advance notice when available generating capacity approaches demand requirements, leveraging forecasted peak load, day-ahead reserve requirements, and net interchange; (2) Attachment O establishing a conditional procedure for emergency use of backup generators (triggered only by DOE Section 202(c) orders) with coordinated PJM and Transmission Owner actions during capacity and transmission emergencies; (3) clarifications separating transmission-security emergency procedures from capacity-based procedures, removing capacity-specific actions (Emergency Bid Process, export recall, capacity load shed) from transmission-security triggers; and (4) updated language for Advanced Scheduled Resources under cold- and hot-weather alerts. Hydro operators must understand the Capacity Advisory's forecasting inputs and threshold logic, as early signals of tight capacity may activate voluntary or mandatory dispatch obligations; pumped-storage operators should note the manual's treatment of generation scheduling during emergencies and any implications for charging-window availability. Most exposed: all dispatchable hydro and PSH participating in PJM's real-time market and ancillary-services offerings. No member comment deadline is stated; the revision was endorsed by the Operating Committee on June 4, 2026.

The revision reorganizes transmission-security emergency procedures to separate them from capacity-focused actions, redefines several alert/action sequences, and adds a new attachment on emergency use of back-up generators. For hydro and PSH operators, Manual 13 defines the operational obligations during emergency conditions—including minimum generation requirements (Attachment H), load-dump capability assessment and allocation (Attachments E, F, N), and dispatch directives for transmission relief—that interact with revenue accrual during scarcity pricing events and state-of-charge management for pumped storage. Operators in the PJM footprint should review Revision 98 for changes to alert sequencing and reserve/generation requirements that may affect their emergency-response positioning and ancillary-service obligations.

initiatives: Flexible Resource Lost Opportunity Costs Eligibility [awaiting senior committee approval]
ai_summary: PJM proposes to refine the definition of "Flexible Resources" to require that all available operating schedules meet the flexibility criteria (combined startup and notification time ≤ 2 hours, minimum run time ≤ 2 hours), rather than permitting flexibility on only some schedules. Under current rules, a unit committed day-ahead on a flexible schedule but holding an inflexible backup schedule can still receive Flexible Resource Lost Opportunity Cost (LOC) credits if not called in real-time, even though it may be unable to start under real-time dispatch due to its inflexible schedule(s). The proposal would classify such units as inflexible for real-time and LOC purposes, restricting LOC eligibility to units that meet flexibility on all schedules and are not called due to transmission or reliability constraints. Tariff and Manual updates (Attachments K, 11, and 28) are under review; the Markets and Reliability Committee is scheduled to endorse the proposal on July 28, 2026, with FERC filing to follow. Fast-start hydro and PSH units with multiple offer schedules are most exposed: those unable to configure all available cost-based schedules as flexible will lose LOC protection and be held to inflexible day-ahead commitments.

ai_summary: PJM is revising Manual M14D to clarify and tighten reactive power (VAR) control requirements for all generators in response to the May 2026 NERC ERO Enterprise CMEP Practice Guide (which lowered IBR registration threshold to 20 MVA/60 kV) and emerging low-voltage stability risks highlighted by the 2025 Spain blackout. The revisions require: (1) generators operate exclusively in automatic voltage-control mode unless documented exceptions are approved by PJM and the Transmission Owner; (2) define acceptable volt-VAR boundaries and VAR control ranges per MW output (32.87% of max MW capacity); and (3) establish a three-party investigative process (PJM, TO, and generator owner/operator) for reactive control performance issues, with PJM empowered to direct AVR and inverter settings changes. For conventional hydroelectric and pumped-storage facilities, this narrows operational flexibility in reactive-power dispatch—generators can no longer operate in constant-MVAR, constant power-factor, or manual modes without PJM/TO approval—potentially reducing the ability to optimize reactive output for revenue or water management. title: Item 02 – Storage As A Transmission Asset – Sata – Phase 2 – Package Summary

ai_summary: PJM's Operating Committee reviewed the Phase 2 framework for Storage as a Transmission Asset (SATA), which allows energy storage (including pumped-storage hydro) to operate as regulated transmission facilities to address localized RTEP violations without participating in competitive markets. Under SATA Phase 2, eligible storage assets would discharge automatically to mitigate identified contingencies, charge via owner coordination afterward, and recover costs through transmission rates (Schedule 12 Transmission Enhancement Credits) rather than market revenue, with metering and telemetry matching standard energy-storage requirements. The framework explicitly prohibits SATA resources from queuing for interconnection or claiming capacity value, and expects assets to be small (≤10 MW) and short-duration (≤4 hours). The document advances to MRC review in July 2026, with FERC submission expected September–November 2026. This creates a new revenue pathway for pumped-storage owners willing to accept regulated-utility-like cost recovery in exchange for operational control and transmission-rate certainty, but forecloses market-participation optionality (energy, AS, capacity) for enrolled assets.

title: Item 03 – 1 Manual 13 – Revision 98 – Presentation
relevance_reason: Manual 13 governs PJM emergency operations procedures that directly affect hydro and other generating resources' obligations during system emergencies, capacity shortages, and transmission security events — particularly dispatch instructions, must-offer requirements, and emergency bid processes that touch hydro revenue and compliance.
stakeholders: Emmanuel Bernabeu (PJM); Mike Handlin (PJM); Paul Dajewski (PJM)
ai_summary: PJM Manual 13 (Emergency Operations), Revision 98, underwent annual review with substantive changes to emergency procedure taxonomy and triggering thresholds effective July 23, 2026. Key changes separate transmission-security emergencies from capacity emergencies, clarify that transmission-security procedures do not trigger Energy Emergency Alerts (EEAs) or Persistent Advisories (PAIs), and add a new Capacity Advisory to provide advance notice when forecasted capacity approaches operating requirements. A new Attachment O codifies procedures for emergency use of backup generators under DOE 202(c) Orders. The revision also updates Advanced Scheduled Resources language for cold/hot-weather alerts and adds RCIS notification to Pre-Emergency Load Management procedures. For hydro operators, the distinction between transmission- and capacity-triggered emergencies affects when they will receive dispatch instructions and emergency bid solicitations — transmission emergencies no longer trigger EEAs, which may narrow the scope of emergency-reserve procurement that traditionally favors hydro's rapid-response capability; the Capacity Advisory may provide earlier signaling of system stress, allowing better strategic positioning. Most affected are large, flexible generators and storage operators participating in PJM's emergency-bid and reserve markets. Revision endorsed by Operating Committee June 4, 2026, with final approval timeline shown through June 24, 2026 (MRC second read).

title: Item 03 – 2 Manual 13 – Revision 98 – Executive Summary

ai_summary: PJM Manual 13 Revision 98 (effective July 23, 2026) introduces a new Emergency Use of Back-up Generators procedure allowing data centers and large loads to disconnect from the grid and operate on-site backup generation during capacity or transmission emergencies—after NERC EEA2 is declared and a DOE 202(c) Order is obtained. PJM will direct Transmission Owners to coordinate disconnection of large loads within 15 minutes, with capacity-deficient control zones exhausting all available large-load capacity before requesting disconnection in zones with excess capacity. This reshapes hydro's strategic value during emergencies: where previously all generation resources (including hydro's full output) would be called to meet contingency reserves, large-load disconnection now becomes an alternative resource, potentially reducing dispatch calls on conventional generators and changing the economic incentive structure for hydro emergency participation. Most exposed are reservoir and pumped-storage operators supplying contingency reserves in constrained zones; run-of-river hydro with fixed output faces less direct impact. The manual becomes effective immediately; no comment deadline is stated.

title: Item 04 – 1 Manual 14d – Revision 71 – Presentation
relevance_reason: PJM's revision to Manual 14d establishes binding reactive power control requirements for all generators, including hydroelectric units, affecting their compliance obligations and operational constraints on voltage support capability provision.
stakeholders: David Mroz (PJM); Ryan Nice (PJM); Emanuel Bernabeu (PJM Operating Committee)
ai_summary: PJM is revising Manual 14d Section 7.1.2 to clarify and strengthen reactive power (voltage support) control requirements for all generators in its footprint, driven by NERC's May 2026 lowering of IBR registration thresholds to 20 MVA and PJM's identification of increasing low-voltage risk (citing the 2025 Spain blackout). The revision mandates automatic voltage control mode as the default for all generators; defines volt-var control boundaries and reactive output ranges tied to MW output; specifies two new required reactive capability curve data points ('Maximum AVR capable MW Output' and 'Unit Minimum MW Output with Reactive Control'); and establishes a three-party investigative process (PJM, transmission owner, generator owner/operator) for reactive control performance issues. For hydroelectric owners, this tightens the operating envelope for reactive power supply: hydro units must now document and receive explicit approval for any AVR mode other than voltage control, and must define their reactive capability limits with new precision, constraining dispatch flexibility and potentially requiring retrofits or AVR reconfiguration on legacy units. The revision proceeds through SOS (June 15), MRC (July 1 and July 9), and OC endorsement (July 23), with education and Q&A sessions between June 4 and July 9. The compliance timeline is not yet stated in this first-read presentation.

ai_summary: PJM is revising Manual 14d (Generator Operational Requirements), sections 7.1.2 and Attachment D, effective July 23, 2026, to add NERC Category 2 GO references, clarify allowable AVR (automatic voltage regulator) modes, specify acceptable volt-var and watt-var control ranges, and formalize PJM's monitoring and engagement authority over reactive-control behavior. The revision responds to NERC's May 2026 Category 2 GO initiative (expanding inverter-based resource reliability standards) and PJM's operational challenges from rising solar/IBR penetration and load growth outstripping generation, both elevating voltage risk. For synchronous hydro and PSH operators, this tightens the specification of reactive-capability dispatch and AVR operating ranges — reducing ambiguity about allowable volt-var curves but also narrowing operational flexibility in voltage control. Most affected are large reservoir hydro and PSH facilities with synchronous generators supplying reactive power in constrained voltage zones; smaller or run-of-river plants with limited reactive margin may face tighter conformance audits. MRC voting is scheduled for July 23rd, 2026.

Key findings show separate regulation products improve ACE (Area Control Error) performance and reliability metrics, though summer conditions remain challenging; improvements stem from changing resource mix and generator movement behavior. The implication for hydro and PSH operators is that the new product structure will change how their regulation capacity awards are determined and priced — previously a single award covered both up and down service; under Phase 2, RegUp and RegDown awards and prices are independently cleared, potentially altering the revenue profile for units providing regulation. title: Informational Only – PJM Esr Model Enhancements Position Paper
relevance_reason: PJM's proposed enhancements to energy storage resource market participation rules—particularly opportunity-cost offer methodology, state-of-charge management, and must-offer requirements—directly affect how pumped-storage hydro and battery storage compete for energy and ancillary-services revenue and how their dispatch is constrained by SOC accounting, setting precedent that will shape storage treatment across RTOs.
ai_summary: PJM staff proposes enhancements to its Energy Storage Resource Participation Model to accommodate rapid battery-storage growth (4,800 MW expected by 2030). The proposal addresses four issue areas: (1) a standardized opportunity-cost calculation for real-time energy offers capping cost at max(incremental energy cost, maximum DA LMP) up to $2,000, with emergency override to $2,000; (2) SOC accounting in day-ahead dispatch (rolling calculation to prevent infeasible dispatch) and ancillary-services clearing (recognizing SOC depletion from AS deployment), but explicit rejection of centralized SOC optimization; (3) no change to inter-day offer rules; and (4) complementary work via the Reserve Certainty Senior Task Force. A stakeholder process begins July 2026. The opportunity-cost cap directly affects how pumped storage (and batteries) offer into real-time markets—tying the cap to max DA LMP rather than real-time conditions or a multiplier makes cost-based offers more predictable but may suppress PSH discharge bids during high-priced hours when SO-C is low. SOC accounting prevents infeasible dispatch but stops short of RTO-led optimization, preserving operator discretion. The proposal affects both standalone storage and MTF configurations (including hydro-battery hybrids). Comments and next steps are embedded in a July 2026 stakeholder launch.
